backends.name: Azure AI Vision Read OCR (Computer Vision)
backends.price_note: As of 2026-06: Free tier (F0) = 5,000 transactions/month, capped at 20 calls/min (also limited to first 2 pages of PDF/TIFF and 4 MB file size). Standard tier (S1) OCR/Read = approx. $1.00 per 1,000 transactions for the 0-1M/month volume tier, with volume discounts at higher tiers (commonly cited around $1.50/1,000 in some regions/older quotes; verify current per-region price on the Azure pricing page, which lists OCR/Read under "OCR (Read)"). One transaction = one image; for documents, page-based billing applies. On-premises Docker container billing follows the same Standard transaction model (requires a billable Azure resource for metering).
backends.free_tier: F0 free tier: 5,000 transactions/month, max 20 transactions/minute; restricted to first 2 pages of multi-page PDF/TIFF and 4 MB max file size.
backends.api_env_var: AZURE_COMPUTER_VISION_ENDPOINT, AZURE_COMPUTER_VISION_KEY (a.k.a. VISION_ENDPOINT / VISION_KEY in Microsoft samples)
backends.python_install: pip install azure-ai-vision-imageanalysis (Image Analysis 4.0 Read; or azure-ai-formrecognizer / azure-ai-documentintelligence for the document-optimized Read model)
backends.languages_note: Printed text: the current GA Read model lists ~127 languages in the official language-support table (older Microsoft docs and third-party sources cite "164"); covers Latin, Cyrillic, Arabic, and Devanagari scripts plus CJK (Chinese Simplified/Traditional, Japanese, Korean). Universal deep-learning models auto-detect language and handle mixed-language text on the same line without a language code. Handwritten text: 9 languages only - English, Chinese Simplified, French, German, Italian, Japanese, Korean, Portuguese, Spanish.
backends.accuracy_note: No standardized benchmark published by Microsoft for the Read engine. Independent 2025 reviews (AIMultiple OCR accuracy benchmark; vendor comparisons) consistently rank Azure's Read/Document Intelligence OCR among the most accurate cloud engines for clean printed text. No public CER/WER figure from Microsoft; OmniDocBench (CVPR 2025) and OCRBench tracks are dominated by VLM-based parsers (e.g. PaddleOCR-VL, GLM-OCR >94% on OmniDocBench) and do not report an official Azure Read score. Treat accuracy as strong for printed/typed text, weaker for low-quality handwriting.
backends.maturity_note: Mature, production GA service (as of 2026-06). Now branded "Azure Vision in Foundry Tools" (formerly Azure AI Vision / Computer Vision). Two current Read editions: Image Analysis 4.0 Read (OCR for images, synchronous, for in-the-wild non-document images) and Document Intelligence Read (asynchronous, for text-heavy scanned/digital documents and PDFs). Legacy Computer Vision v3.2 GA Read and v2.1 RecognizeText are explicitly not recommended (no further updates to v3.2). Docs last updated 2025-11-21; actively maintained.
backends.speed_note: Image Analysis 4.0 Read is a fast synchronous API designed for near real-time, single-image UX scenarios. Document Intelligence Read is asynchronous (submit then poll) and optimized for batch/large documents up to 2,000 pages.
backends.privacy_note: Cloud API: image/document data is sent to Microsoft's Azure region; governed by Azure/Foundry Tools data policies (no use of customer data to train models by default; transient processing). On-premises option: a Distroless Docker container (Read v3.2 GA capabilities) can run fully in your own environment for data-governance/air-gapped needs, though it still requires a billable Azure resource for metering.
pros: Synchronous Read 4.0 API returns OCR plus other image insights in one call, easy to embed in real-time UX
Broad language coverage (~127 printed languages across Latin, Cyrillic, Arabic, Devanagari, CJK) with automatic mixed-language detection - no language code needed
Handwriting recognition for 9 languages, returned with per-word confidence and bounding polygons
On-premises Docker container available for data-residency / air-gapped deployments
Backed by Azure SLA, scale, compliance, and SDKs for multiple languages (Python, C#, JS, Java); document path handles up to 2,000-page PDFs/TIFFs
cons: Proprietary, closed-source; requires an Azure account and sends data to the cloud unless you run the (still-metered) container
Plain Read engine does not extract math/LaTeX, charts, or barcodes; tables and key-value pairs require the separate Document Intelligence Layout/prebuilt models (extra cost/complexity)
Handwriting limited to 9 languages and degrades on poor-quality cursive
Confusing/forking product surface: split between Image Analysis 4.0 Read, Document Intelligence Read, and deprecated v3.2 - easy to pick the wrong edition
Per-transaction pricing and free-tier caps (5,000/mo, 2-page PDF limit) can get costly at document scale; no fully free self-hostable option
backends.best_for: Cloud applications already on Azure that need reliable printed-text (and some handwritten) extraction from images and PDFs across many languages, with bounding boxes and confidence scores - especially real-time UX scenarios (Read 4.0) or batch document processing (Document Intelligence Read).

backends.name: Calamari OCR
backends.vendor: Calamari-OCR project (originated at University of Würzburg, Center for Philology and Digitality / Christoph Wick, Christian Reul et al.); community-maintained
backends.price_note: Free and open source (no paid tier, no hosted service). As of 2026-06: zero cost; only your own compute (CPU/GPU). Pretrained models are free downloads.
backends.free_tier: Entirely free — full functionality with no usage limits; self-hosted only.
backends.python_install: pip install calamari-ocr
backends.accuracy_note: From the Calamari paper (arXiv:1807.02004): CER 0.11% on the UW3 dataset (modern English) and 0.18% on the DTA19 dataset (German Fraktur), reported to outperform OCRopy/Tesseract on those line-level historical/printed benchmarks. Gains come largely from confidence voting across a 5-fold model ensemble plus pretraining. No OmniDocBench/OCRBench scores exist (those target full-page/LLM document OCR; Calamari is a line recognizer, not a layout/document engine, so it is not represented there). Accuracy applies to clean, segmented single text lines in trained scripts; degrades on unseen scripts/fonts without fine-tuning.
backends.languages_note: No fixed language list — Calamari is script/alphabet-agnostic and trains on any character set. In practice it is used overwhelmingly for Latin-script material. Official pretrained mixed models (calamari_models repo) cover: historical Antiqua and Fraktur (German blackletter, 15th-19th c.), modern English (uw3-modern-english), 18th-19th c. French, and an idiotikon model with broad Latin-based diacritics suitable for several modern European languages. CJK, Arabic, Cyrillic, and Indic are not provided out of the box but can be trained by the user.
backends.speed_note: Fast at inference on single lines; CNN-LSTM models run on CPU and accelerate on GPU. Voting (5-fold ensemble) multiplies inference cost ~5x vs single model. No page-level pipeline, so throughput depends on an external line-segmentation step.
backends.privacy_note: Fully local/on-prem. No data leaves the machine; no network calls or API keys. Ideal for sensitive archives.
backends.maturity_note: ~1.2k GitHub stars, ~209 forks (as of 2026-06). Latest release v2.3.1 on PyPI dated 2024-11-12; v2.x line is the current TensorFlow 2 generation. Development has slowed markedly (low commit/release cadence in 2025); the project is stable and usable but not under heavy active development. Academic origin (Univ. of Würzburg digital humanities).
pros: State-of-the-art line-level accuracy on printed/historical text (CER ~0.1-0.2% on benchmark sets) via 5-fold ensemble confidence voting plus pretraining
Fully free, open source, and 100% local — no API keys, no per-page cost, complete data privacy
First-class trainability: cross-fold training, data augmentation, and fine-tuning let you adapt to any script/alphabet or specific historical fonts
Free pretrained mixed models for Antiqua, Fraktur, modern English, and historical French; integrates with eScriptorium/OCR4all and PageXML/ABBYY/HDF5 workflows
Usable both as a clean Python library and a CLI, with per-character confidence scores
cons: Line recognizer only — no page layout analysis, no reading-order detection, no line segmentation; you must supply pre-segmented text lines (e.g. via OCRopy nlbin / OCR4all / eScriptorium)
No tables, math/formulas, charts, barcodes, or key-value extraction; plain-text transcription only
GPL-3.0 license (copyleft) — not Apache-2.0; can complicate use in closed-source/commercial products
Out-of-the-box models are almost entirely Latin-script historical print; non-Latin scripts and modern documents typically require training your own model
Heavy TensorFlow dependency and slowing maintenance; setup is heavier than lightweight engines and lags behind modern transformer/LLM document-OCR systems for general-purpose use
No hosted/SaaS option, no bounding-box output, and voting multiplies inference time
backends.best_for: Digital-humanities and library/archive projects doing high-accuracy transcription of printed and historical documents (especially Latin-script Antiqua/Fraktur) where you can pre-segment lines and want a free, trainable, fully local engine — often as the recognition backend inside OCR4all or eScriptorium.

backends.name: Camelot
backends.vendor: camelot-dev (open-source community; originally Vinayak Mehta / SocialCops)
backends.price_note: Free and open source (MIT), no usage fees or quotas. As of 2026-06. Self-hosted; only your own compute costs apply (GPU optional for the [ml] Table Transformer backend).
backends.free_tier: Fully free — unlimited local use; no API, no metering.
backends.python_install: pip install "camelot-py"  (extras: pip install "camelot-py[ml,ocr,plot,ghostscript]")
backends.accuracy_note: Camelot is a table-EXTRACTION tool, not a character-recognition OCR engine, so CER/WER and OmniDocBench/OCRBench do not apply. In the arXiv comparative study "A Comparative Study of PDF Parsing Tools Across Diverse Document Categories" (2410.09871, Table 5, table-detection F1), Camelot scored highly on bordered/ruled tables but poorly on complex ones: Tender 0.8279 (best, beating Tabula 0.4619, pdfplumber 0.5580, Table Transformer@0.6 IoU 0.7496), Manual 0.5975, Law 0.3861, Scientific 0.3392, Financial 0.1012, Patent 0.0181. Performance is highly document-type dependent and strong only when tables have clear lines/structure.
backends.languages_note: Language-agnostic for native text-based PDFs: it reads the PDF's embedded text layer (via pdfium/Ghostscript/poppler), so it handles whatever scripts the PDF encodes (Latin, CJK, Cyrillic, Arabic, etc.) without per-language models. For scanned PDFs the optional [ocr] extra uses RapidOCR (rapidocr-onnxruntime), which supports Latin, Chinese (Simplified/Traditional), Japanese, Korean and more; no single documented count for Camelot itself.
backends.speed_note: Fast on native text PDFs (pure-Python geometric parsing of the embedded text layer; lattice/stream/network parse pages in well under a second to a few seconds each on CPU). The optional [ml] Table Transformer backend and [ocr] (RapidOCR) path are much slower and benefit from a GPU; both are lazily imported so a plain import camelot never loads PyTorch/OCR.
backends.privacy_note: Fully on-premise / offline. Runs entirely on your machine; no data is sent anywhere and no API key is required. Default pdfium backend ships as a bundled wheel with no network calls. Ideal for sensitive/confidential documents.
backends.maturity_note: Mature and actively maintained. ~3.8k GitHub stars, ~541 forks, ~1,479 commits (camelot-dev/camelot). Latest release v2.0.0 on 2026-06-04 (preceded by 1.0.x line: 1.0.0 Dec 2024, 1.0.9 Aug 2025). The camelot-dev fork is the maintained successor to the original (atlanhq) repo. As of 2026-06.
pros: Best-in-class for ruled/bordered tables in native text-based PDFs; lattice parser reliably reconstructs cell grids and beats Tabula on lattice cases
Multiple complementary parsers (lattice, stream, network, hybrid, plus optional ML/Table Transformer) and an 'auto' selector, so you can tune per document type
Reports per-table quality metrics (accuracy + whitespace) and confidence scores, enabling automated filtering of bad extractions without manual review
Free, MIT-licensed, fully offline/on-prem — no API keys, no per-page cost, good for confidential data
Default pdfium backend is a bundled wheel with zero system dependencies; rich export to DataFrame/CSV/JSON/Excel/HTML/Markdown/SQLite
Heavy deps (PyTorch, OCR) are optional extras and lazily imported, keeping the core install light
cons: NOT a general OCR engine — designed for text-based PDFs; scanned/image PDFs only work via the optional [ocr] extra, and it does not handle plain images, handwriting, math, or general document text
Accuracy is highly document-type dependent: collapses on borderless, nested, color-coded, or irregular tables (e.g. F1 0.0181 on patents, 0.1012 on financial docs in the arXiv study)
Stream parser for borderless tables often needs manual tuning (table_areas, columns, edge_tol) to get usable output
The strong [ml] Table Transformer path adds large PyTorch/transformers/timm dependencies and benefits from a GPU
Only extracts tables — gives no full-page reading order, prose text, or broader document structure (pair it with a separate text extractor for that)
backends.best_for: Extracting tabular data from born-digital, text-based PDFs (financial reports, government/tender filings, scientific papers, manuals) into pandas DataFrames or CSV/JSON/Excel — especially tables with visible gridlines (lattice). Best when you need a free, offline, scriptable tool with quality metrics, and can tune parameters per document type.
backends._verify_notes:
All volatile claims re-verified against primary sources (GitHub camelot-dev/camelot and PyPI camelot-py) as of 2026-06.

CONFIRMED:
- License MIT / open_source true: confirmed on both GitHub repo page and PyPI.
- pricing_model free_oss / free_tier: MIT, self-hosted, no API/metering. Accurate. The [ml] extra does pull in PyTorch (Table Transformer backend), matching the GPU-optional note.
- maturity_note: ~3.8k stars, 541 forks, 1,479 commits confirmed on GitHub. v2.0.0 released 2026-06-04 confirmed on both GitHub and PyPI. backends.name: DeepSeek-OCR
backends.price_note: Free, open-weights (MIT). No first-party hosted API or per-page price; the only cost is your own GPU compute. Paper cites throughput of ~200k+ pages/day on a single A100-40G. As of 2026-06, third-party hosts (Hugging Face inference providers, Replicate, API aggregators) may charge to serve it, but there is no official DeepSeek OCR endpoint.
backends.free_tier: Entirely free to download and self-host (weights on Hugging Face under MIT). No quota or rate limit; the only constraint is your own GPU.
backends.python_install: pip install torch==2.6.0 torchvision==0.21.0 transformers==4.46.3; pip install flash-attn==2.7.3 --no-build-isolation (optional: vLLM 0.8.5 for high-throughput serving)
backends.accuracy_note: OmniDocBench (model card): overall 75.7, Arxiv Math 77.2, Old Scans Math 73.6. Paper: ~97% OCR decoding precision at <10x text/vision-token compression, ~60% at 20x. Fox benchmark: 98.5% exact-match at 6.7x compression (600-700 text tokens / 100 vision tokens), 96.8% at 9.7x, ~59.1% at ~19.7x with only 64 tokens. On OmniDocBench it surpasses GOT-OCR2.0 using only 100 vision tokens/page and beats MinerU2.0 (6000+ tokens/page) with under 800 vision tokens. (A successor "DeepSeek-OCR 2", arXiv 2601.20552, reports ~91.09% on OmniDocBench v1.5 — a separate, newer model.)
backends.languages_note: Reported to support OCR in nearly 100 languages, including low-resource/minority scripts (e.g., Arabic, Sinhala). Covers Latin, CJK (Chinese/Japanese/Korean), Arabic, Cyrillic, and Indic scripts; Chinese and English are the primary, best-tested languages. Per-language quality is not individually benchmarked.
backends.speed_note: High throughput for an OCR VLM: ~2500 tokens/s per A100-40G via vLLM; paper cites ~200k+ pages/day on a single A100-40G for bulk data generation. Speed scales with chosen resolution mode (fewer vision tokens = faster). Single-image latency on consumer GPUs is modest but slower than classic CPU OCR like Tesseract.
backends.privacy_note: Fully on-prem / air-gappable: weights run locally, no data leaves the machine when self-hosted. Privacy depends entirely on your deployment; using a third-party host would send documents to that provider.
backends.maturity_note: Released Oct 20, 2025 by DeepSeek AI. GitHub repo highly popular (tens of thousands of stars); HF model card showed ~2.3M downloads in a recent month — very high adoption. Active ecosystem; a successor DeepSeek-OCR 2 paper appeared by early 2026. As of 2026-06 the original remains widely used and integrated (transformers, vLLM).
pros: Open weights under permissive MIT license; fully self-hostable and air-gappable with no per-page fees
Novel 'context optical compression' yields very strong accuracy-per-token: matches/beats GOT-OCR2.0 and MinerU2.0 using far fewer vision tokens
Structured document output: markdown, HTML tables, LaTeX math, SMILES for chemical structures, plus grounding/bounding-box localization
Very high bulk throughput (~200k+ pages/day on one A100-40G), ideal for large-scale document-to-text pipelines
Selectable resolution modes (Tiny/Small/Base/Large/Gundam) trade tokens vs accuracy for cost control
Broad language coverage (~100 languages incl. minority scripts) for a single open model
cons: Requires an NVIDIA GPU (CUDA); heavier and slower per-image than classic CPU OCR engines like Tesseract
Pinned, somewhat fragile dependency stack (specific torch 2.6 / transformers 4.46.3 / flash-attn / vLLM 0.8.5 versions) can make setup finicky
No native per-token confidence scores, complicating downstream quality gating
As a generative VLM it can hallucinate or drop content, especially at high compression ratios (accuracy falls to ~60% at 20x)
No official hosted API/SLA — you own all serving, scaling, and ops
Handwriting and some edge cases are not first-class; primary strength is printed/structured documents in Chinese/English
backends.best_for: Large-scale, GPU-backed document-to-markdown/text conversion where you want an open, self-hostable model with strong structured output (tables, math, charts) and excellent token-efficiency — e.g., building LLM training corpora or on-prem document pipelines.

backends.name: Docling
backends.vendor: IBM Research (Zurich) / LF AI & Data Foundation (docling-project)
backends.price_note: Free and open-source (MIT). No usage fees. As of 2026-06 the only costs are your own compute/GPU. Models (layout, TableFormer, GraniteDocling VLM, EasyOCR/RapidOCR weights) download once and are cached locally at no cost. Remote OCR backends it can wrap (e.g. Apple Vision on macOS, or a KServe inference server you host) are themselves free; any third-party paid OCR would be billed separately by that provider.
backends.free_tier: Entirely free; no tier limits. Runs fully offline/air-gapped after model download.
backends.python_install: pip install docling
backends.is_local_note: Runs locally; can operate in completely isolated air-gapped environments (per official FAQ). Model weights downloaded once then cached.
backends.privacy_note: Strong privacy: runs entirely on-machine and is documented as usable in fully isolated/air-gapped environments with no remote calls. Data does not leave the machine unless you explicitly configure a remote OCR backend (e.g. the optional KServe inference-server option). Default OCR engines (EasyOCR, RapidOCR, Tesseract, OcrMac/Apple Vision) are all local.
backends.accuracy_note: Docling is a layout+OCR pipeline rather than a single OCR model, so OCR accuracy depends on the chosen backend (Tesseract/EasyOCR/RapidOCR/Apple Vision). Strong third-party benchmark (Procycons PDF Data Extraction Benchmark, 2025): 97.9% accuracy on complex hierarchical tables (47/48 cells) and ~100% on dense technical text, judged "the most robust framework for processing complex business documents" vs Unstructured and LlamaParse. Docling's own DocLayNet (layout) and TableFormer (table structure) models are reported state-of-the-art in the Docling Technical Report (arXiv:2408.09869). On OmniDocBench, Docling was added to the evaluation set in Jan 2026 but does not appear among the top end-to-end pipeline scores; VLM pipelines like MinerU2.5 (overall ~90.67, text edit distance ~0.047) currently lead — no single Docling OmniDocBench edit-distance figure is published in the public leaderboard. No standardized CER/WER number for Docling itself.
backends.speed_note: Per Docling Technical Report (arXiv:2408.09869): ~481 ms/page on an NVIDIA L4 GPU (~2.1 pages/s), ~1.26 s/page on Apple M3 Max (~0.79 pages/s), ~3.1 s/page on x86 CPU (~0.32 pages/s). Third-party benchmark: ~6.3 s for a single page and ~65 s for 50 pages with roughly linear scaling. OCR-heavy or full-page-OCR modes are slower; GPU substantially speeds layout/table/VLM stages.
backends.languages_note: Language coverage is inherited from the pluggable OCR backend, not Docling itself. Tesseract supports 100+ languages (with installable language packs); EasyOCR ~80+ languages (Latin, CJK — Chinese/Japanese/Korean, Arabic, Cyrillic, Devanagari/Indic, Thai, etc.); RapidOCR maps ISO-639 codes onto three bundled model sets — English, Chinese, and a shared "latin" model set (de/fr/es etc. fall back to latin to preserve inter-word spacing); OcrMac/Apple Vision covers the languages Apple's framework supports (macOS only). Effective union is dominated by Tesseract's 100+ when that backend is installed.
backends.maturity_note: Very mature and highly active as of 2026-06: ~62k GitHub stars, ~4.3k forks, latest release ~v2.104.0 (June 2026), frequent releases. Originated at IBM Research Zurich; now a hosted LF AI & Data Foundation project (docling-project org). Large ecosystem with LangChain/LlamaIndex/Haystack integrations.
backends.best_for: Self-hosted, privacy-sensitive document-to-structured-content conversion at scale: converting PDFs/DOCX/PPTX/XLSX/HTML/images into clean Markdown or lossless JSON for RAG and gen-AI pipelines, with strong table, layout, formula, and code extraction. Best when you need pluggable OCR (swap Tesseract/EasyOCR/RapidOCR/Apple Vision) and full offline/air-gapped operation rather than a hosted API.
pros: MIT-licensed, fully local/air-gapped capable — no per-page fees and data never leaves the machine
Pluggable OCR backends (Tesseract, EasyOCR, RapidOCR, Tesseract-CLI, OcrMac/Apple Vision, optional remote KServe) selectable per pipeline
Rich structured output beyond plain text: layout/reading order, table structure (TableFormer), formulas, code blocks, chart-to-table, plus Markdown/JSON/HTML/DocTags export
Strong real-world extraction quality (97.9% on complex tables in an independent benchmark) and very broad input-format support (PDF, Office, HTML, EPUB, images, even audio/email)
Extremely active, well-funded project (IBM + LF AI & Data, ~62k stars) with first-class RAG framework integrations
cons: OCR accuracy is only as good as the chosen backend — Docling adds no proprietary OCR model, so it can trail dedicated VLM OCR pipelines (e.g. MinerU2.5) on raw text edit-distance benchmarks
CPU-only throughput is modest (~0.3 pages/s on x86); a GPU is effectively needed for high-volume or VLM/GraniteDocling workloads
Handwriting support is weak/undocumented — depends entirely on the backend (EasyOCR/Apple Vision handle some; Tesseract poor)
Heavier and more complex to install/operate than a single OCR binary (multiple model downloads, PyTorch/ONNX deps); first run pulls large models
No hosted/managed API or SLA — you own deployment, scaling, and updates
RapidOCR language handling is coarse (collapses many languages into one shared 'latin' model set), and per-engine language packs must be managed manually

backends.name: docTR
backends.vendor: Mindee (now maintained by t2k GmbH with Mindee support)
backends.price_note: Free and open source (Apache-2.0); no license, subscription, or per-page fees. Only cost is your own compute/hosting. As of 2026-06. (Mindee also sells a separate commercial document-AI API, but docTR the library is free.)
backends.free_tier: Fully free — unlimited local use, no API key or quota.
backends.python_install: pip install python-doctr (or pip install "python-doctr[viz,html,contrib]")
backends.accuracy_note: Author-published benchmarks on FUNSD/CORD (from the official "Choosing the right model" docs). Text recognition exact-match: crnn_vgg16_bn 88.21% (FUNSD) / 95.47% (CORD); parseq 88.53% / 95.56%; master 88.57% / 95.73%. Text detection (recall/precision): db_resnet50 ~83.6%/86.7% (FUNSD), 92.6%/86.4% (CORD); fast_base ~85.0%/86.7% (FUNSD), 94.4%/85.4% (CORD). Best end-to-end OCR combo db_resnet50+master ~73.9% recall/76.7% precision (FUNSD), 85.8%/80.1% (CORD). Docs claim competitiveness with Google Vision / AWS Textract. No independent OmniDocBench/OCRBench score found for docTR; FUNSD/CORD are small (FUNSD ~199 pages) so treat as indicative, not definitive.
backends.languages_note: No single documented count. Default pretrained recognition models use a Latin (originally "french") vocabulary covering Latin-script Western European languages (English, French, German, etc.). Built-in vocabularies also exist for additional scripts/languages including Cyrillic (Russian, Ukrainian), Hebrew, Hindi/Bengali/Gujarati (Indic), Vietnamese, and others; broader coverage requires selecting/loading the right vocab or fine-tuning. Community multilingual checkpoints (e.g. a parseq multilingual model covering ~12 languages) are available on Hugging Face. CJK is not well covered out of the box.
backends.maturity_note: Mature and active. Latest release v1.0.1 on 2026-02-04 (v1.0.0 was the major release that dropped TensorFlow). ~6.1k GitHub stars, ~649 forks, 1000+ commits on main. Originated at Mindee; now primarily maintained by t2k GmbH with Mindee support. As of 2026-06.
backends.speed_note: Optimized for both CPU and GPU inference. Lightweight combos run on CPU; GPU gives large speedups for batch/throughput. Recognition speed varies widely by model: viptr_tiny is very fast (~0.08 sec/it), parseq moderate (~2.2 sec/it), master slowest (~17.6 sec/it at batch 64). Default detector switched to fast_base for speed in recent versions. ONNX deployment available via the companion OnnxTR project for faster, dependency-light inference.
backends.privacy_note: Fully on-premise / local — runs entirely on your own hardware, no data leaves the machine. Models download once from the hub on first use, then inference is offline. Strong fit for sensitive/regulated documents.
pros: Free, Apache-2.0, fully local — no per-page cost and no data leaves the machine, good for privacy/regulated workloads
Modular two-stage architecture: mix-and-match detection (DBNet, LinkNet, FAST) and recognition (CRNN, SAR, MASTER, ViTSTR, PARSeq, VIPTR) backbones to trade speed vs accuracy
Simple 3-lines-of-code API; outputs a structured Page/Block/Line/Word document with bounding boxes and per-word confidence scores
Handles PDFs and images, rotated/skewed pages, and offers a KIE predictor for class-based extraction (addresses, dates, etc.)
Benchmarks competitive with Google Vision / AWS Textract on FUNSD/CORD; can run on CPU and accelerate on GPU, with ONNX export via OnnxTR
Actively maintained (v1.0.1, Feb 2026), well-documented, with pretrained weights and training/fine-tuning support
cons: No built-in math/LaTeX, table-structure, chart, or barcode recognition — it is word-level OCR, not full document understanding

Out-of-the-box language coverage is Latin-centric; other scripts (Cyrillic, Indic, Hebrew, CJK) need the right vocab, community models, or fine-tuning, and there is no single documented language count
Handwriting is not a focus — primarily tuned for printed/scanned documents
TensorFlow backend was removed in v1.0.0; now PyTorch-only, so the 'PyTorch or TensorFlow' framing applies only to pre-1.0 versions
Benchmarks are author-published on small datasets (FUNSD ~199 pages); no independent OmniDocBench/OCRBench numbers, so real-world accuracy may vary by document type
Markdown/DOCX/hOCR-style rich exports are not first-class — outputs are JSON/text/XML plus visualization; downstream layout-to-markdown work is on you
backends.best_for: Developers needing a free, self-hosted, privacy-preserving OCR pipeline for printed PDFs and document images, who want word-level text plus bounding boxes and confidence in structured JSON, and who value swappable detection/recognition models and Python integration over turnkey table/math/handwriting extraction.

PyTorch as the default and only deep learning backend." Stars 6,147 (~6.1k ✓), forks 649 (✓). backends.name: dots.ocr
backends.price_note: The model itself is free (MIT, open weights) — self-host with no licensing cost. There is no official first-party paid API; pricing comes only from third-party hosts (as of 2026-06): Replicate ~$0.0032 per run (community sljeff/dots.ocr deployment); Chutes lists it at ~$0.01 / 1M input tokens and ~$0.01 / 1M output tokens, pay-as-you-go with no subscription. Self-hosting cost is just GPU compute.
backends.free_tier: Fully free to self-host (open weights, MIT). Free live demo at dotsocr.xiaohongshu.com and Hugging Face Spaces. Third-party hosts (Replicate/Chutes) are pay-as-you-go with no perpetual free tier beyond trial credits.
backends.python_install: pip install dots-ocr (from repo: pip install -e . ; runs via Hugging Face Transformers or vLLM >=0.9.1, vLLM officially integrated in 0.11.0+)
backends.api_env_var: REPLICATE_API_TOKEN (if using Replicate) or CHUTES_API_KEY (if using Chutes); none required for self-hosting
backends.accuracy_note: Strong, peer-reported benchmarks. OmniDocBench v1.0 (overall text edit distance, lower=better): dots.ocr 0.032 EN / 0.066 ZH, beating Gemini 2.5 Pro (0.055 EN / 0.168 ZH) and GPT-4o (0.144 EN / 0.409 ZH). Table TEDS 88.6 EN / 89.0 ZH (vs Gemini 2.5 Pro 85.8/86.4). Formula edit distance 0.329 EN / 0.416 ZH; reading-order edit 0.040 EN / 0.067 ZH. Reported SOTA on text/tables/reading order for its size. The successor dots.mocr (3B, March 2026) reports olmOCR-bench 83.9±0.9 and ranks #2 after Gemini 3 Pro on the OCR Arena Elo leaderboard. Source: official Hugging Face model card and arXiv:2512.02498.
backends.languages_note: Documented multilingual benchmark spans 100 languages with emphasis on robust low-resource-language parsing. Covers Latin, CJK (Chinese simplified/traditional, Japanese, Korean), Cyrillic (Russian), Arabic, Indic (e.g. Kannada), Tibetan, and many other scripts; marketed as able to recognize "virtually any human script."
backends.best_for: Self-hosted, cost-free, privacy-preserving end-to-end document parsing where you want one compact model to do layout detection, reading order, tables, formulas, and multilingual text extraction with structured JSON+bbox output — competitive with proprietary VLM OCR services without per-page fees.
backends.speed_note: Single ~3B VLM; one forward pass does layout + recognition. Reported ~2 pages/sec on GPU via vLLM; throughput depends heavily on GPU and page complexity. Officially optimized through vLLM integration (0.11.0+).
backends.privacy_note: Fully self-hostable with open MIT weights, so documents need never leave your infrastructure — strong fit for on-prem/air-gapped and sensitive-data use. Data only leaves the machine if you opt into a third-party host (Replicate/Chutes) or the public Xiaohongshu demo.
backends.maturity_note: Actively maintained, popular: ~8.9k+ GitHub stars (up from ~4.3k in late 2025). Original dots.ocr (~3B) released July 2025; arXiv paper 2512.02498 (Dec 2025); evolved to dots.ocr-1.5 and rebranded dots.mocr (March 2026), with a dots.mocr-svg variant. As of 2026-06, rapidly iterating.
pros: Open weights under permissive MIT license — free to self-host, fine-tune, and deploy commercially with no per-page cost
Unifies layout parsing, reading order, tables, formulas, and multilingual text recognition in a single compact ~3B VLM (simpler pipeline than multi-stage OCR stacks)
Benchmark-competitive with or beating much larger proprietary services (Gemini 2.5 Pro, GPT-4o) on OmniDocBench text/tables/reading order
Broad multilingual coverage (100-language benchmark, strong on low-resource scripts)
Structured JSON output with bounding boxes plus Markdown/HTML/LaTeX; officially integrated into vLLM for efficient serving
Privacy-friendly: documents can stay fully on-prem
cons: Requires a GPU for practical throughput; no CPU-friendly path
No official first-party hosted API or SLA — remote use relies on third-party hosts (Replicate, Chutes) of varying reliability
As a generative VLM it can hallucinate/omit content and provides no per-token confidence scores
Original model does not parse pictures/embedded images within documents; complex tables and formulas remain challenging (acknowledged limitations)
Fast-moving naming/versioning (dots.ocr → dots.ocr-1.5 → dots.mocr) can complicate reproducibility and pinning
Handwriting is not a documented strength; results on handwritten input are unreliable
backends._verify_notes:
All volatile/decision-critical claims re-verified against primary sources (GitHub rednote-hilab/dots.ocr, HF model card, Replicate, Chutes) as of 2026-06; no corrections needed.

CONFIRMED:
- license=MIT, open_source=true (GitHub repo + HF card).
- languages_count=100 (dots.ocr-bench = 1493 PDF images across 100 languages; marketed 100+).
- GitHub stars ~8.9k currently (consistent with record's "~8.9k+, up from ~4.3k late 2025").
- Original dots.ocr released 2025.07.30; arXiv/HF paper 2512.02498 (Dec 2025) confirmed for the original model.

backends.name: EasyOCR
backends.price_note: Free and open source (Apache-2.0); no usage fees, no API. Models download once at first use. As of 2026-06 there is no hosted/paid tier from Jaided AI for the library itself; Jaided AI offers separate paid custom-model training/enterprise support engagements (quote-based), not a metered OCR API.
backends.free_tier: Entirely free — unlimited local use, no account or key required.
backends.python_install: pip install easyocr
backends.languages_note: Officially marketed as "80+ languages"; documentation enumerates ~86 languages across 6 script families: Latin (English, Spanish, French, German, etc.), Chinese (simplified + traditional), Cyrillic (Russian, Ukrainian, etc.), Arabic (Arabic, Persian, Urdu), Devanagari/Indic (Hindi, Marathi, Nepali, etc.), plus standalone scripts like Japanese, Korean, Thai, Tamil, Telugu, Kannada, Bengali. Languages sharing a script can be recognized together in one pass.
backends.accuracy_note: No single standardized vendor benchmark published. EasyOCR was added to OmniDocBench's OCR/text-recognition track (Jan 2025) but as a text-line recognizer, not a full doc-parsing model, so no headline OmniDocBench overall score is reported for it (modern VLMs lead that board at ~90%+). Independent comparisons report relative CER/WER: EasyOCR typically achieves lower CER than PaddleOCR but higher WER (good character recognition, weaker word segmentation); on one handwritten-notes test EasyOCR CER ~0.16 vs PaddleOCR ~0.24. Tesseract often edges it on clean printed scans. Strong on scene/natural-image text where it generally beats Tesseract.
backends.speed_note: Moderate. CPU inference is slow on large/high-DPI images; GPU (CUDA) gives a large speedup and is recommended for batch or real-time use. Model init/load ~2.8s (vs ~0.3s Tesseract, ~4.2s PaddleOCR in one benchmark). PyTorch-based.
backends.privacy_note: Fully on-device/on-prem — runs locally, no data leaves the machine. Only network access is a one-time download of detection/recognition model weights at first use (can be pre-staged for air-gapped deployment).
pros: Truly ready-to-use: pip install plus a 3-line script, sensible defaults, auto-downloads models
Broad multilingual/multi-script coverage (~86 languages, all major scripts) in one lightweight library
Returns bounding boxes AND per-detection confidence scores, useful for downstream filtering/layout
Permissive Apache-2.0 license; fully local/offline so no data leaves the machine and no per-page cost
Strong on scene/natural-image text (CRAFT detector), often outperforming Tesseract on photos/signage
Supports custom/fine-tuned recognition models for domain-specific text
cons: No built-in table extraction, layout analysis, key-value, or math/formula recognition — plain text + boxes only
Handwriting support is experimental/limited, not production-grade
Slow on CPU for large images; effectively needs a GPU for throughput
Word-level segmentation can be weak (higher WER), and it can struggle on dense full-page documents vs purpose-built doc parsers
Maintenance has slowed — last release v1.7.2 (Sep 2024), with a sizeable open-issue backlog as of 2026-06
No reading-order/structured document output (Markdown/HTML/ALTO/hOCR not supported)
backends.maturity_note: Mature and very popular (~30k GitHub stars, ~3.6k forks as of 2026-06) but slowing: latest release v1.7.2 on 2024-09-24 (23 releases total), with several hundred open issues and a community fork (easyocr2, v1.0.1 Dec 2025) emerging to address compatibility. PyTorch-based; requires Python 3, torch + torchvision.
backends.best_for: Local, offline, multilingual extraction of text + bounding boxes from images and scene/photo text where a permissive license and zero per-page cost matter, and where tables/forms/math/structured layout are NOT required.

backends.name: GOT-OCR2.0
backends.vendor: Haoran Wei et al. (UCAS / StepFun / Megvii); weights published under the stepfun-ai HuggingFace org
backends.license: Apache-2.0 (code and model weights); training data released CC-BY-NC-4.0
backends.price_note: Free open-weights model (Apache-2.0). No first-party paid or hosted API. As of 2026-06 you self-host the ~580M-param weights and pay only your own compute. Third-party hosts (e.g. Clarifai listing under stepfun-ai/ocr, or community Replicate/fal-style endpoints) may charge per call, but those are unofficial and pricing varies by provider.
backends.free_tier: Fully free — open weights, run locally with no usage caps or token limits.
backends.python_install: pip install transformers torch accelerate (optional: verovio for sheet-music rendering; vllm or sglang for serving). Model id: stepfun-ai/GOT-OCR-2.0-hf (Transformers-native) or stepfun-ai/GOT-OCR2_0 (original)
backends.languages_note: Primarily English and Chinese (the Qwen-based decoder is strong in both; the Fox benchmark used for evaluation is EN/CN). The Transformers HF model card is tagged "multilingual" and the architecture can be fine-tuned to other scripts, but no fixed documented language count exists, and out-of-the-box coverage of Arabic, Cyrillic, Indic, etc. is unverified/weak. Confirmed scripts: Latin (English), CJK (Chinese).
backends.accuracy_note: From the GOT paper (arXiv:2409.01704), on the Fox document-OCR benchmark GOT reaches edit distance ~0.035 (English) and ~0.038 (Chinese) with F1 ~0.97-0.98, competitive with much larger models at its Sept-2024 release. On chart OCR it reported outperforming chart-specialist models (OneChart, ChartVLM). However, on the newer OmniDocBench v1.5 leaderboard (2025-2026) it is no longer SOTA: current top models (GLM-OCR 94.6, PaddleOCR-VL-1.5 94.5, MinerU 2.5 90.7, dots.ocr 88.4) substantially exceed GOT-class models; GOT-OCR2.0 is not listed among current leaders. No single standardized cross-engine CER/WER figure is published; treat the paper's Fox numbers as the canonical benchmark.
pros: Genuinely unified single 580M model: one checkpoint handles plain text, math/molecular formulas, tables, charts, sheet music and geometric shapes (markdown/LaTeX/TikZ/SMILES/Kern output)
Truly open and self-hostable: Apache-2.0 weights, first-class HuggingFace Transformers integration (~200K downloads/month as of 2026-06), runs offline with zero per-page cost and full data privacy
Small and efficient relative to multi-billion-param VLMs, yet strong document-OCR accuracy (Fox edit distance ~0.035 EN / ~0.038 CN)

Useful advanced features: interactive region OCR by bounding-box coordinates or color, dynamic-resolution patch cropping for odd aspect ratios, and native multi-page OCR producing one continuous output
Multiple serving paths (Transformers, vLLM, SGLang) plus community ONNX/MNN/GGUF/llama.cpp ports for varied hardware
cons: No longer state-of-the-art: 2025-2026 models (GLM-OCR, PaddleOCR-VL, MinerU 2.5, dots.ocr, DeepSeek-OCR) clearly outperform it on OmniDocBench v1.5
Effectively English+Chinese only out of the box; other scripts need fine-tuning and there is no documented language list
GPU strongly recommended (designed for CUDA; bf16/fp16 inference) — CPU-only use is slow and impractical for volume

Weak on handwriting; primarily targets printed/man-made optical characters

backends.name: img2table
backends.price_note: Free and open-source (MIT) as of 2026-06. No cost for the library itself. Note: cloud OCR backends it can plug into (AWS Textract, Google Vision, Azure) are billed separately by those providers; local backends (Tesseract, PaddleOCR, EasyOCR, docTR, Surya, RapidOCR) are free.
backends.free_tier: Entire library is free; no usage limits. Only metered if you opt into a paid cloud OCR backend.
backends.python_install: pip install img2table (extras: img2table[paddle], [easyocr], [doctr], [surya], [rapidocr], [gcp], [aws], [azure])
backends.accuracy_note: No standardized OmniDocBench/OCRBench/CER/WER benchmark published by the project. Table detection is pure-OpenCV (deterministic) so quality depends on document type; text content accuracy is entirely determined by the chosen OCR backend. Informal third-party comparisons report ~95-99% on clean printed/bordered tables, but dedicated neural table tools (e.g. commercial extractors) lead on complex merged-cell/borderless/multi-level-header layouts (~90-97%). The README explicitly notes OpenCV-only detection has limitations and works best on white/light backgrounds; tables with no recoverable OCR data are not returned.
backends.languages_note: No fixed language count — language support is inherited from the chosen OCR backend. Tesseract covers 100+ languages/scripts (Latin, CJK, Arabic, Cyrillic, Indic, etc.); PaddleOCR, EasyOCR, docTR, Surya, RapidOCR and the cloud APIs each bring their own coverage. img2table itself is script-agnostic for the geometric table-structure detection step.
backends.speed_note: Lightweight and CPU-friendly for the table-detection stage (pure OpenCV, with Cython/numba-optimized line detection). Overall throughput is gated by the chosen OCR backend: Tesseract/RapidOCR run fast on CPU, while EasyOCR/PaddleOCR/docTR/Surya are faster with a GPU. Suitable for batch PDF/image processing without specialized hardware.
backends.best_for: Extracting structured tables (including merged cells and borderless layouts) from images and PDFs into pandas DataFrames or Excel, on CPU-only infrastructure, with freedom to pick any OCR backend (local or cloud). Good fit when you need a free, self-hosted, pluggable table extractor rather than a full document-understanding model.
pros: Pure-OpenCV table detection: lightweight, deterministic, runs well on CPU with no GPU and no ML model download
Pluggable OCR layer — Tesseract, PaddleOCR, EasyOCR, docTR, Surya, RapidOCR plus cloud (AWS Textract, Google Vision, Azure) — so you choose cost/accuracy/language trade-off
Handles complex structures: merged cells, semi-bordered and borderless tables, implicit rows/columns, and skew up to ~45 degrees
Clean Python ergonomics: tables returned as objects with pandas DataFrames, cell-level bounding boxes, plus direct Excel (.xlsx) and HTML export preserving structure
Permissive MIT license, free, fully self-hostable — no data leaves the machine when using a local OCR backend
cons: Scope is table extraction only — not a general OCR engine, no plain-page text, no math/formula or chart understanding
Detection quality is OpenCV-bound: degrades on dark/colored backgrounds, low-quality scans, and very complex multi-level headers
Text accuracy is only as good as the external OCR backend; tables with no recoverable OCR data are silently dropped
No published standardized benchmark (no OmniDocBench/OCRBench/CER numbers) and no built-in confidence scores
Single-maintainer open-source project (~875 GitHub stars); reliant on third-party OCR libraries that add heavy/native dependencies
backends.privacy_note: Fully on-prem / self-hostable. With a local OCR backend (Tesseract, PaddleOCR, EasyOCR, docTR, Surya, RapidOCR) no data leaves the machine. Only if you opt into a cloud OCR backend (AWS Textract, Google Vision, Azure Cognitive Services) is document data sent to that third party.

backends.license: Apache-2.0 (InternVL3.5); MIT (InternVL3). Note: variants built on Qwen2.5/Qwen3 inherit those base-model licenses (mostly Apache-2.0).

backends.name: Keras-OCR
backends.price_note: Free and open source (MIT). No fees, no API, no quotas. Only cost is local compute (GPU recommended for throughput). As of 2026-06.
backends.free_tier: Entirely free; runs fully on local hardware with no usage limits.
backends.python_install: pip install keras-ocr
backends.accuracy_note: No standardized OmniDocBench/OCRBench score published. The repo's own benchmark on the first 1,000 COCO-Text validation images (IoU>=0.5, text similarity>=0.5) reports end-to-end precision ~0.50-0.53 and recall ~0.54-0.59 (depending on scale), with latency ~417-699ms/image on a Tesla P4 GPU. These are scene-text-in-the-wild numbers; accuracy is decent for clean horizontal English scene/print text but degrades on dense documents, small fonts, and the recognizer is case- and punctuation-blind by default. Source: keras-ocr README/docs benchmark table.
backends.languages_note: English only out of the box (Latin script). The pretrained CRNN recognizer's DEFAULT_ALPHABET is string.digits + string.ascii_lowercase (36 chars: 0-9 plus a-z), so it ignores uppercase and all punctuation. CRAFT detection is script-agnostic, but recognition for other languages/scripts requires training a new recognizer on your own alphabet/data (community forks exist for Korean, etc.).
backends.speed_note: Moderate; GPU strongly recommended for batches. ~0.4-0.7s/image end-to-end on a Tesla P4 GPU in the repo benchmark; substantially slower on CPU. TensorFlow startup and first-call weight download add overhead.
backends.privacy_note: Fully local/on-prem. No data leaves the machine at inference time. Pretrained weights are auto-downloaded from the maintainer's hosting on first use (one-time network access), after which it runs offline.
backends.maturity_note: ~1.5k GitHub stars. Latest PyPI release 0.9.3 on 2023-11-06; the last GitHub tagged release shown is older (v0.8.4, 2020-09-13). No new releases in ~2.5 years as of 2026-06 and many open issues (~100+), so it is mature but effectively in low-maintenance/quasi-dormant status. Pinned to legacy TensorFlow 2.x APIs; compatibility-maintained community forks (e.g. geo-tp/image-ocr) exist for newer Python/TF.
backends.best_for: Self-hosted, free English scene/printed-text detection+recognition where you want word-level bounding boxes and the option to fine-tune the detector or recognizer end-to-end on your own data, and where case/punctuation insensitivity and Latin-only output are acceptable.
pros: Completely free, MIT-licensed, fully local/offline after first weight download — no API keys, quotas, or data egress
Pairs a strong text detector (CRAFT) with a CRNN recognizer behind a simple high-level Pipeline API (a few lines to get word + bounding box results)
Includes a full end-to-end training pipeline with synthetic data generation, so you can fine-tune the detector and/or recognizer on custom alphabets, fonts, or domains
Returns word-level bounding box polygons, convenient for downstream layout/annotation work
cons: Effectively stalled: no new release since 0.9.3 (Nov 2023), pinned to legacy TensorFlow 2.x, with many unresolved open issues — install/compatibility friction on modern Python/TF stacks
Default recognizer is English-only and case- and punctuation-insensitive (alphabet = 0-9 + lowercase a-z); anything else requires retraining
No document understanding: no tables, no math, no reading-order/layout, no handwriting, no confidence scores
Accuracy is only fair on dense documents/small text and trails modern engines (e.g. PaddleOCR, docTR, VLM-based OCR); no standardized OmniDocBench/OCRBench results
Heavy dependency footprint (TensorFlow + OpenCV + imgaug) and GPU effectively needed for reasonable throughput

backends.name: Kraken
backends.vendor: Benjamin Kiessling / Ecole Pratique des Hautes Etudes (EPHE-PSL); community-maintained (GitHub: mittagessen)
backends.price_note: Free and open source (Apache-2.0); no license fee or per-page cost as of 2026-06. The engine, training pipeline, and the freely-licensed model repository are all free. Only real cost is self-provided compute: a Nvidia GPU with ~8GB+ VRAM is recommended for training generalized models from scratch, while fine-tuning and inference run on CPU (much slower). There is no official paid/hosted Kraken API; the closest "service" is a self-hosted or institution-hosted eScriptorium instance, which is itself free OSS.
backends.free_tier: Entire engine is free with unlimited local use. Free pretrained recognition and segmentation models are downloadable via `kraken get <DOI>` from the Zenodo / HTRMoPo repository.
backends.python_install: pip install kraken (PDF support: pip install kraken[pdf])
backends.accuracy_note: No standardized cross-engine benchmark (OmniDocBench/OCRBench) reports Kraken directly, since it targets historical/non-Latin material outside those modern-document benchmarks and accuracy is model-dependent. Real-world results: with a model trained on the target material, Kraken reaches state-of-the-art HTR/OCR quality and consistently outperforms Tesseract on challenging historical texts. Published CER figures for Kraken-trained models in the digital-humanities literature commonly fall in the low single digits to ~10% CER depending on script, hand, and training-set size (e.g. printed and CATMuS Medieval models achieve a few percent CER on in-domain data). For loose comparison, related HTR systems on similar historical material report ~8-10% CER (PyLaia ~10.3%, Transkribus Titan ~8.0%). The ICDAR 2025 paper "Version 5 of the Kraken ATR Engine for the Humanities" documents added trainable reading order and unsupervised recognition pretraining but does not publish a single headline CER. Out-of-the-box (untrained) on arbitrary modern documents, accuracy is weaker than turnkey engines.
backends.languages_note: Script/language-agnostic by design: there is no fixed language count, because recognition quality depends on the loaded model rather than built-in language packs. Strong emphasis on historical and non-Latin scripts. The freely-licensed model repository and community models cover Latin/Fraktur (blackletter, older European typefaces), Greek (incl. early printed/polytonic), Hebrew, Arabic script (including Persian, Ottoman Turkish, Urdu, Jawi), Syriac, Cyrillic (incl. Serbian), and various Indic scripts (Devanagari for Hindi, Bengali). Native support for Right-to-Left, bidirectional (BiDi), and top-to-bottom / vertical scripts (e.g. Arabic, Hebrew, Mongolian). Models are tagged with ISO 15924 script codes and ISO 639-3 language codes.
backends.maturity_note: Mature and actively maintained as of 2026-06. Latest release v7.0.2 (2026-05-04, a security hotfix); ~1,000 GitHub stars, ~164 forks, ~2,394 commits. Forked from OCRopus, long lineage in the DH community. Developed at EPHE-PSL, funded by EU programs (ATRIUM, ERC MiDRASH). Tightly integrated as the recognition engine behind the widely-used eScriptorium training/annotation UI. v5 (ICDAR 2025) added trainable reading order, unsupervised pretraining, and the HTRMoPo model repository schema.
backends.speed_note: CPU inference is workable but slow; a Nvidia GPU greatly accelerates both training and recognition. Neural layout analysis is more robust but slower than projection-profile segmentation. Throughput depends on chosen network size (smaller VGSL models trade accuracy for speed). Not designed for high-volume, low-latency production OCR; oriented to careful batch processing of archival material.
backends.privacy_note: Fully local / on-premises. Runs entirely on the user's machine or self-hosted server (incl. self-hosted eScriptorium); no data leaves the machine and no external API calls during recognition. Model downloads from Zenodo are optional and one-time. Strong fit for sensitive or rights-restricted archival collections.
backends.best_for: Digitizing historical manuscripts and early printed books, and non-Latin / low-resource scripts (Arabic, Hebrew, Syriac, Greek, Indic, Fraktur), where you can train or fine-tune a custom model on your material. The default engine for digital-humanities and library/archive HTR workflows, especially via eScriptorium.
pros: State-of-the-art for historical and non-Latin scripts; fully trainable layout analysis, reading order, and recognition, so it adapts to material mainstream engines fail on
Native right-to-left, bidirectional, and vertical/top-to-bottom script support (Arabic, Hebrew, Mongolian, etc.) that most OCR engines lack
Rich structured output (ALTO, PageXML, abbyyXML, hOCR) with per-character bounding boxes/polygons and 0-1 confidence scores, ideal for archival pipelines
Free and Apache-2.0 with a public Zenodo/HTRMoPo repository of freely-licensed models retrievable via `kraken get`
Fully local/on-prem -> strong privacy for sensitive collections; integrates with the eScriptorium UI for collaborative training and transcription
Configurable network architectures via a VGSL spec language plus a plugin system, giving fine control over speed/accuracy trade-offs
cons: Not plug-and-play: out-of-the-box accuracy on arbitrary modern documents is mediocre; getting good results usually requires finding or training a model on your material
Training generalized models from scratch needs significant compute (GPU with ~8GB+ VRAM) and substantial transcribed ground truth
No built-in broad multilingual coverage like Tesseract/PaddleOCR; you depend on the available model for each script
No math/formula or chart/diagram understanding; table extraction only emerges indirectly from layout + coordinates, not as structured tables
Comparatively slow, especially on CPU and with neural layout analysis; not suited to high-throughput, low-latency production OCR
Smaller ecosystem and steeper learning curve (VGSL, segmentation models, training data prep); primarily a DH/archival tool rather than a general SDK

NOTE: Groq deprecated/decommissioned its Llama 3.2 Vision (11B/90B) preview endpoints on 2025-04-07 in favor of Llama 4 Scout, so Groq no longer serves these models. backends.accuracy_note: Meta-reported (instruction-tuned): DocVQA(ANLS) 88.4 (11B) / 90.1 (90B); ChartQA(relaxed) 83.4 (11B) / 85.5 (90B); TextVQA(val) 73.1 (11B); AI2D 91.1 (11B). These are document-VQA/chart tasks, not pure transcription CER/WER. Meta did not publish an official OCRBench/OmniDocBench score; independent comparisons consistently place Llama 3.2 Vision BELOW Qwen2-VL/Qwen2.5-VL and InternVL on OCRBench (e.g. Qwen2.5-VL-7B ~86 OCRBench vs Llama 3.2 trailing). No standardized CER/WER benchmark found for raw OCR. Source: HF model card; Artificial Analysis; community OCRBench comparisons.
backends.languages_note: 8 officially supported languages for TEXT tasks (English, German, French, Italian, Portuguese, Hindi, Spanish, Thai). For image+text (the OCR/vision path), Meta officially supports ENGLISH ONLY; other languages/scripts (CJK, Arabic, Cyrillic, Indic beyond Hindi) may work informally but are not validated and quality degrades. Primarily Latin-script document OCR.
backends.speed_note: Generative VLM: slower and more compute-heavy than dedicated OCR engines (token-by-token decode). 11B runs on a single ~24GB GPU (quantized fits smaller); 90B needs multi-GPU / large memory (~160GB+ in BF16) or a hosted endpoint. Hosted providers like Groq give low-latency inference; throughput is per-image, not batched-page OCR.
backends.privacy_note: Fully self-hostable — data never leaves your machine/VPC when run locally via transformers/vLLM/Ollama. Using a hosted provider (Bedrock, Groq, Together, Fireworks, OpenRouter) sends images to that third party under their terms.
backends.maturity_note: Released Sept 25, 2024 by Meta. Mature, widely adopted open-weight VLM with broad ecosystem support (transformers, vLLM, SGLang, Ollama, llama.cpp, many hosted providers). Popular community OCR wrapper: Nutlope/llama-ocr (PDF/image to Markdown). As of 2026-06 it is superseded on OCR leaderboards by newer VLMs (Qwen2.5-VL, Qwen3-VL, InternVL3.x) but remains a stable, well-supported baseline.
backends.best_for: Teams that want an open-weight, self-hostable multimodal model for document understanding, chart/table reasoning, and English document-to-Markdown OCR where layout reasoning and Q&A matter more than character-perfect transcription — and who want to avoid sending data to a third party.
pros: Open-weight and self-hostable (transformers, vLLM, SGLang, Ollama, llama.cpp) — data can stay fully on-prem with no per-page/API fees
Strong document-VQA and chart/diagram reasoning (DocVQA 88-90 ANLS, ChartQA 83-85, AI2D 91) — understands content, not just transcribes it
Outputs structured text directly: Markdown tables, JSON, key-value extraction via prompting — no separate layout pipeline needed
Broad hosted-provider availability (Bedrock, Groq, Together, Fireworks, OpenRouter) for those who prefer an API; competitive token pricing (~$0.72/1M for 90B)
11B variant runs on a single mid-range GPU, making local OCR/document Q&A practical without huge infra
cons: Not a transcription-optimized OCR engine: hallucinates/invents text more than GPT-4o and dedicated OCR; needs human review for critical extraction
Image+text officially English-only; weak/unvalidated on non-Latin scripts (CJK, Arabic, Cyrillic) — poor multilingual OCR coverage
No bounding boxes, no confidence scores, no character-level positions — unsuitable for precise layout/coordinate-dependent workflows
Trails newer open VLMs (Qwen2.5-VL, Qwen3-VL, InternVL3) on OCRBench and pure text-reading tasks
90B is heavy to self-host (multi-GPU / ~160GB+); slower and costlier per page than purpose-built OCR engines like Tesseract or PaddleOCR
Struggles with empty table cells, dense/complex charts, and fine handwriting

Strong choice when you need GPT-4o-class OCR locally on a laptop, a single mid-range GPU, or even a phone (4.6).
pros: Open-weight (Apache-2.0) and runs fully on-device/offline — no per-page cost and strong privacy; INT4/AWQ/GGUF quants run on CPU, single GPU, or phones
Excellent OCR/document benchmarks for its size: 4.5 (8B) reports OCRBench 89.0, DocVQA 94.7, and SOTA OmniDocBench document parsing among general MLLMs, claiming to beat GPT-4o-latest/Gemini 2.5
Handles high-resolution any-aspect images (up to ~1.8M px) with ~4x fewer visual tokens, plus tables, math/LaTeX, handwriting, charts, multi-image and video in one model
Broad deployment ecosystem (Transformers, vLLM, SGLang, llama.cpp, Ollama) and native mobile support (iOS/Android/HarmonyOS) with open edge code
Optional OpenAI-compatible hosted API with a free public key (4.6) lowers the barrier to trying it without local setup
Multilingual (30+ languages) with very strong Chinese + English coverage
cons: It is a general MLLM, not a purpose-built OCR engine: no built-in word/line confidence scores, and bounding-box/grounding output requires prompting and is less reliable than dedicated OCR engines
Generative VLM OCR can hallucinate or omit text on dense/noisy pages, and outputs are non-deterministic; needs validation for high-stakes extraction
The newest 4.6 (1.3B) trades capability for size — lower knowledge recall and weaker per-task numbers than 4.5 (8B); standardized OCR benchmarks for 4.6 are not yet published
Self-hosting the 8B model for good throughput effectively needs a GPU; CPU/quantized inference is slower than classic OCR engines for bulk pages
Hosted API pricing, quotas, and rate limits are undocumented, and the free key + China-based endpoint (api.modelbest.cn) raise reliability/data-residency questions for production
No native barcode/QR or sheet-music recognition; not specialized for those modalities

backends.name: MMOCR
backends.price_note: Free and open source (Apache-2.0). No license, subscription, or per-page fees. As of 2026-06, the only cost is your own compute/GPU. No hosted/managed API is offered by the project.
backends.free_tier: Entirely free; self-hosted with no usage limits.
backends.python_install: pip install -U openmim && mim install mmengine mmcv mmdet && mim install mmocr (officially installed via OpenMIM; pip install mmocr also exists but mim is recommended to resolve the mmcv/mmdet binary chain)
backends.accuracy_note: Reproduces published SOTA-era results from its model zoo (word accuracy, MMOCR 1.0 docs): recognition - ABINet IIIT5K 0.96 / SVT 0.94 / IC13 0.95 / IC15 0.81; SATRN 0.96 / 0.92 / 0.96 / 0.80; SAR 0.95 / 0.88 / 0.94 / 0.76; NRTR 0.95 / 0.88 / 0.95 / 0.76; CRNN 0.81 / 0.81 / 0.87 / 0.56. Detection (ICDAR2015 hmean-iou): DBNet-R18 0.8169, DBNet-R50+oCLIP 0.8644, FCENet-R50+oCLIP 0.8604. These are strong scene-text numbers but reflect 2021-2023 architectures; MMOCR does not appear in modern document-parsing leaderboards (no OmniDocBench/OCRBench score for the toolbox itself, since those evaluate end-to-end VLMs/parsers, not component detector+recognizer toolboxes). Sources: MMOCR model zoo docs.
backends.languages_note: No single documented language count. Core pretrained models target English/Latin scene text; a Chinese recognition config/model is provided. Because it is a training toolbox, language coverage is determined by the character dictionary and training data you supply, so it can in principle be trained for any script (Latin, CJK, etc.). Out-of-the-box multilingual coverage is far narrower than dedicated engines like Tesseract or PaddleOCR.
backends.best_for: Researchers and ML engineers who want to train, fine-tune, benchmark, or compose state-of-the-art scene text detection / recognition / spotting / KIE models under a unified, modular, config-driven PyTorch framework - rather than teams wanting a turnkey document OCR product.
pros: Broad model zoo under one config-driven API: detection (DBNet/DBNet++, PANet, PSENet, FCENet, TextSnake, DRRG, Mask R-CNN), recognition (CRNN, SAR, SATRN, NRTR, ABINet, ASTER, MASTER, RobustScanner, SVTR), end-to-end spotting (ABCNet, ABCNetv2, SPTS), and KIE (SDMG-R)
Apache-2.0, fully self-hostable with no fees, no data leaving the machine - good for privacy-sensitive and offline use
Modular OpenMMLab design lets you swap backbones/necks/heads and mix detector+recognizer freely; strong for research, ablation, and custom training
Reproducible published benchmark numbers and ready dataset preparers (Dataset Preparer) lower the barrier to fair comparisons
Inference gives word/line bounding polygons plus per-prediction confidence scores
cons: Effectively in maintenance-only / stagnant state: last release v1.0.1 was July 2023, with no new releases since; the broader OpenMMLab ecosystem has wound down active development
Heavy, brittle install chain (mmengine + mmcv + mmdet via OpenMIM) that is sensitive to exact PyTorch/CUDA versions - notoriously hard to set up
Not a document-OCR/layout product: no native table extraction, no math/formula recognition, weak reading-order/layout analysis, and limited multilingual out-of-the-box models
GPU strongly recommended for practical throughput; transformer recognizers (SATRN, NRTR) are slow/heavy on CPU
Aimed at researchers - more code and configuration required than turnkey engines; not ideal if you just want text out of a scanned PDF
Pretrained models reflect 2021-2023 architectures and have been overtaken by newer VLM-based document parsers on complex/document benchmarks
backends.speed_note: Throughput depends heavily on chosen model and hardware. Lightweight pipelines (DBNet + CRNN) are fast on GPU; transformer recognizers (SATRN, NRTR, ABINet) are slower and memory-heavy. CPU inference is workable for small jobs but markedly slower; GPU is recommended for batch workloads.
backends.privacy_note: Fully local/self-hosted; no data leaves the machine and no network calls are required for inference. Suitable for on-prem and air-gapped deployments.
backends.maturity_note: ~4.7k GitHub stars; ~20 releases, latest v1.0.1 on 2023-07-04 (v1.0.0 on 2023-04-06). No releases since mid-2023 and minimal recent commit activity - effectively maintenance/legacy mode as of 2026-06, consistent with the wider OpenMMLab project's reduced activity. Not archived. As-of date: 2026-06.

backends.name: Nougat
backends.vendor: Meta AI (Facebook Research) — author Lukas Blecher et al.
backends.price_note: Free and open source (MIT code). No hosted/paid API offered by Meta. Costs are self-hosted compute only (GPU recommended). As of 2026-06, weights remain CC-BY-NC-4.0, so commercial use of the released weights is restricted by license.
backends.free_tier: Fully free — pip install nougat-ocr; weights downloaded from Hugging Face. No quotas; non-commercial weight license is the only restriction.
backends.python_install: pip install nougat-ocr (extras: pip install "nougat-ocr[api]")
backends.accuracy_note: In the original paper (arXiv:2308.13418, Table 1), Nougat-base on its held-out academic-PDF test set: overall normalized edit distance 0.071, BLEU 89.1, METEOR 93.0, F1 93.1; plain text edit-dist 0.058 / F1 95.7; math edit-dist 0.128 / F1 76.5; tables edit-dist 0.211 / F1 78.0. Nougat-small is comparable (overall edit-dist 0.073). Both substantially beat GROBID and embedded-PDF-text baselines. These are strong on clean, single-column English scientific papers but degrade on out-of-distribution layouts. No standardized public-leaderboard number found: Nougat is referenced as a baseline in OmniDocBench (CVPR 2025) but does not appear in its current end-to-end leaderboard tables, and it is absent from the IDP/OmniDocBench v1.5 leaderboard (as of 2026-06).
backends.speed_note: Slow: autoregressive Swin-encoder + mBART-decoder generation. ~19.5 s per batch (~1400 tokens); batch of 10 pages maximizes A100 throughput; model load can take ~15 s on A100. Far slower than classical pipelines (GROBID ~10.6 PDF/s). GPU strongly recommended; CPU is impractical for volume.
backends.languages_note: English only in practice. Docs: "works best with English papers, other Latin-based languages might work. Chinese, Russian, Japanese etc. will not work." No multilingual claim; no documented language count. (Third-party fine-tunes like Arabic-Nougat exist but are separate models.)
backends.best_for: Converting born-digital or scanned English scientific/academic PDFs into Mathpix-Markdown (.mmd) with inline LaTeX math and tables — e.g. building markdown/LaTeX corpora from papers for RAG, search, or ML training where preserving equations matters.
pros: OCR-free end-to-end transformer: reads rasterized pages directly, so it works on scanned/image-only PDFs with no embedded text layer
Strong LaTeX math and table reconstruction — a key differentiator over classical OCR and GROBID (math F1 ~76, plain-text F1 ~96 on its test set)
Fully open source (MIT code) and self-hostable with no API keys, quotas, or data leaving the machine — good for private/sensitive documents
Simple, multi-surface deployment: CLI, Python library, and a FastAPI REST endpoint (nougat_api) out of the box
Outputs clean Mathpix-Markdown that maps directly to markdown/LaTeX downstream
cons: English-only in practice; explicitly does not handle Chinese/Russian/Japanese, and non-academic document types are out of scope
Slow autoregressive generation; needs a GPU for any real volume and is far slower than pipeline tools
Prone to hallucination/repetition loops and [MISSING_PAGE] dropouts; failure-detection heuristic is unreliable on CPU/older GPUs
Effectively unmaintained: last PyPI release 0.1.17 (Oct 2023), no updates since; image-to-text pipeline path is now broken in transformers v5 (needs direct model load or transformers 4.x)
Model weights are CC-BY-NC-4.0 — non-commercial only — so the released weights cannot be used commercially without retraining
No bounding boxes, confidence scores, or general document-region/reading-order layout output
backends.privacy_note: Fully on-premise: runs locally, weights are downloaded once from Hugging Face, and no document data leaves the machine during inference. Good fit for confidential documents.
backends.maturity_note: facebookresearch/nougat ~9-10k+ GitHub stars; original release Aug 2023, last PyPI release 0.1.17 on 2023-10-04 — no releases since, effectively dormant. facebook/nougat-base on Hugging Face still heavily used (~170k+ downloads/month as of mid-2026) and integrated into the transformers library, but the upstream repo is not actively developed. As-of 2026-06.

backends.name: OCR4all
backends.vendor: OCR4all project / University of Würzburg (Center for Philology and Digitality, ZPD), with OCR-D collaboration
backends.price_note: Free and open-source under MIT license. No subscriptions, no paywalled features, no usage fees. Self-hosted, so the only cost is your own compute/hardware. (As of 2026-06.)
backends.free_tier: Entirely free — full functionality with no tiers or limits beyond your own hardware.
backends.python_install: N/A — distributed as a Docker image (e.g. `docker run -p 1476:8080 ... ocr4all/ocr4all`), not a pip package. Underlying engines (Calamari) are pip-installable separately.
backends.privacy_note: Fully self-hosted; runs locally via Docker on your own machine/server. No data leaves the machine — well suited for sensitive or archival material. No external API calls required for core OCR/HTR.
backends.languages_note: No fixed published language count — it is an engine-agnostic platform whose language coverage comes from the underlying recognizers (Calamari, Kraken) and from trainable/pretrained models. Documented strengths: historical Latin-script European languages (German incl. Fraktur and Antiqua, Latin, French, Dutch, English) from the 15th–19th century, plus a "polyfont"/mixed model covering many typographies. Kraken integration extends to other scripts (e.g. Arabic, right-to-left, etc.). Handles Unicode peculiarities like long-s (ſ) and combining diacritics when present in training data. Custom models can be trained for any script with ground truth.
backends.accuracy_note: No OmniDocBench/OCRBench entry (those target general/LLM OCR, not historical-print pipelines). Published research benchmarks: with suitable mixed/pretrained models, OCR4all reaches CER below 0.5% on early printed books for non-expert users; on fully-automatic 19th-c. novels it averaged ~0.85% CER vs ABBYY FineReader's ~5.3% (Reul et al., Appl. Sci. 2019). Its main engine Calamari reports CER 0.155% on UW3 (modern English) and 0.221% (0.184% with voting) on DTA19 (19th-c. German Fraktur). Accuracy depends heavily on model fit / available ground truth for training.
backends.speed_note: Throughput depends on hardware and the chosen engine; Calamari/Kraken are TensorFlow/PyTorch deep-learning recognizers that benefit from a GPU but run on CPU. Designed for batch/mass full-text recognition of printings as well as careful single-document work, so it is workflow-oriented rather than optimized for low-latency single-page calls.
backends.maturity_note: Mature open-source academic project from the University of Würzburg (MIT license), tied to the German OCR-D initiative. GitHub OCR4all/OCR4all has ~708 stars, but the main application repo is now largely dormant: its latest release is 0.6.1 (Jan 28, 2022), preceded by 0.6.0 (Jan 26, 2022, which added Kraken baseline layout analysis and Calamari 2.x support) and 0.5.0 (Nov 7, 2020, which added a REST API and DOCX export). The repo's last code push was Feb 2024. A next-generation OCR-D-aligned rewrite (ocr4all-app / ocr4all-backend / ocr4all-libraries-frontend) was attempted but those repos are now archived (late 2024). As of 2026-06 the only actively developed component is the LAREX layout-analysis tool and its new LAREX Action SDK (pushed June 2026). Not archived or deprecated, but the OCR4all application itself is effectively in maintenance/dormant status; usable today but not under fresh feature development. (As of 2026-06.)

backends.name: ocrmac (Apple Vision)
backends.vendor: Maximilian Strauss (community); wraps Apple Vision framework
backends.price_note: Free and open-source (MIT). No usage fees of any kind — OCR runs on-device via Apple's Vision framework, which ships free with macOS. Only cost is owning a Mac. As of 2026-06.
backends.free_tier: Fully free; unlimited local use. No API key, no quota, no metering.
backends.python_install: pip install ocrmac
backends.accuracy_note: No standardized benchmark (OmniDocBench/OCRBench/CER/WER) found for ocrmac specifically. It exposes Apple's Vision OCR, which independent OCR studies rate as strong on printed/typed text (commonly placed near Google Cloud Vision and well above Tesseract on noisy/real-world images). No published, reproducible CER/WER figure exists for the ocrmac wrapper itself; quality tracks the installed macOS version's Vision/LiveText models.
backends.speed_note: On an M3 Max MacBook Pro (per README): fast ~131 ms/image, accurate ~207 ms/image, livetext ~174 ms/image. On-device, no network latency; throughput scales with Apple Silicon Neural Engine.
backends.languages_note: Languages are whatever the installed macOS Vision build supports (query via supportedRecognitionLanguages). Recent macOS supports ~18 recognition languages spanning Latin (English, French, German, Spanish, Italian, Portuguese), CJK (Simplified/Traditional Chinese, Japanese, Korean), Cyrillic (Russian, Ukrainian), and Arabic scripts. The `fast` recognition level supports fewer languages than `accurate`. Set via `language_preference` using IANA/BCP-47 codes (e.g. en-US, zh-Hans, de-DE). Count varies by macOS version.
backends.best_for: Fast, free, fully on-device OCR of printed text from images on macOS — batch image-to-text pipelines, screenshot/photo text extraction, privacy-sensitive workloads where data must not leave the machine, and developers already on Apple Silicon who want word/line text plus confidence and bounding boxes without external services.
pros: Completely free and offline — Apple Vision ships with macOS, no API key, quota, or per-page cost
Fully on-device: images never leave the machine (strong privacy / data-residency story)
Fast on Apple Silicon (~130-210 ms/image) with no network latency
Returns text plus per-element confidence and normalized bounding boxes out of the box
Two backends: classic Vision (fast/accurate levels) and the newer, stronger LiveText (macOS Sonoma+)
Tiny, MIT-licensed, simple API (ocrmac.OCR('img.png').recognize()); supports ~18 languages incl. CJK/Cyrillic/Arabic
cons: macOS-only — no Linux, Windows, or cloud/server deployment without a Mac host
No table extraction, no math/formula recognition, no markdown/structured-document output — plain text + boxes only
Handwriting is only partially supported (depends on macOS version's models) and undocumented in the wrapper
No published, reproducible accuracy benchmark for the wrapper; quality is tied to the installed macOS version and not independently versioned
LiveText backend ignores recognition_level/confidence_threshold and always reports confidence 1.0
Language set and capabilities change silently with macOS upgrades — not fully under the developer's control
backends.privacy_note: Excellent privacy posture: all OCR runs locally on-device through Apple's Vision framework. No data is sent to any server or third party; there is no cloud component. Naturally on-prem since it only runs on the user's Mac.
backends.maturity_note: ~522 GitHub stars; latest release v1.0.1 on 2026-01-08; actively maintained (reached 1.0). PyPI classifier: Beta. Single primary maintainer. As of 2026-06.
