backends.name: OCRopus / ocropy
backends.vendor: Thomas Breuel / DFKI (originally Google-sponsored); community on GitHub (ocropus / ocropus-archive)
backends.price_note: Free and open source (Apache-2.0). No paid tier, no hosted service. Self-hosted only; you pay only for your own compute. As of 2026-06.
backends.free_tier: Fully free — entire engine is OSS with no usage limits.
backends.python_install: git clone https://github.com/ocropus-archive/DUP-ocropy && cd DUP-ocropy && pip install -r requirements.txt && python setup.py install  (Python 2.7 only; no PyPI wheel; original ocropus/ocropy repo was archived & moved to ocropus-archive/DUP-ocropy on 2026-04-27)
backends.accuracy_note: Strong on clean printed text for its era; no standardized modern benchmark (no OmniDocBench/OCRBench entry). Published research numbers: the LSTM line recognizer reached ~0.6% CER on English from the UW3 database, and ~0.40% CER on German Fraktur vs ~2% for the older ISRI/segment-based voting approach (Breuel et al., "High-Performance OCR for Printed English and Fraktur using LSTM Networks", 2013). Successor Calamari later reached ~0.11% CER on UW3, illustrating that ocropy is now outperformed by its descendants.
backends.speed_note: CPU-only (classic ocropy has no GPU path); LSTM line recognition is relatively slow and single-threaded per line. Layout analysis and binarization add overhead. Adequate for batch corpora, not for high-throughput production.
backends.languages_note: Script-agnostic LSTM+CTC recognizer (no language model needed); accuracy depends entirely on the trained model. Ships an English (en-default) model; a Fraktur/German model is downloadable. Community/research models exist for Latin, Greek, Cyrillic, Sanskrit, Devanagari, Urdu and other scripts. No fixed "N languages" count — you train your own model per script/typeface.
backends.maturity_note: Lineage announced 2007; Python ocropy with LSTM recognizer reached v1.0 in Nov 2014; last release 1.3.3 (Dec 2017). GitHub ~3.5k stars. The main ocropus/ocropy repo was ARCHIVED (read-only, no longer maintained) on 2026-04-27 and moved under ocropus-archive (DUP-ocropy). Breuel's PyTorch-era successors ocropus3 (PyTorch 0.3, now broken/obsolete) and ocropus4 exist but are experimental/research-grade, not maintained as products. Effectively legacy/dormant as of 2026-06.
backends.privacy_note: Fully local/on-prem; no data leaves the machine. Nothing is sent to any server.
backends.best_for: Historical and early-printed-book OCR pipelines where you train a custom line model per typeface/script, and academic/digital-humanities work that needs a transparent, fully local, trainable LSTM line recognizer. In practice, new projects should use its successors (Kraken, Calamari, OCR4all).
pros: Fully open source (Apache-2.0), self-hosted, no data leaves the machine and no usage costs
Pioneering, transparent LSTM+CTC line recognizer that is script-agnostic and trainable on your own data without a language model
Modular CLI pipeline (binarization → page segmentation → line recognition → hOCR) you can mix and match
Excellent on clean printed and historical/Fraktur text for its era (~0.4–0.6% CER in published studies); foundational ancestor of Kraken and Calamari with strong DH community knowledge
Outputs hOCR with line/word bounding boxes and per-line confidence, convertible to searchable PDF
cons: Repository was archived (read-only) on 2026-04-27 — no maintenance, no bug fixes, no support
Classic ocropy is Python 2.7 ONLY and explicitly refuses Python 3, making installation painful on modern systems
Largely superseded — Kraken, Calamari and OCR4all give better accuracy, Python 3, GPU support and active maintenance
Not a turn-key OCR system: 'a collection of document analysis programs' requiring manual per-typeface model training; weak on all-caps, symbols, super/subscripts
No tables, math, charts, barcodes, handwriting-as-a-feature, or full reading-order/document-structure output; CPU-only with no GPU acceleration
No PyPI package, no hosted API, no standardized modern benchmark coverage (absent from OmniDocBench/OCRBench)

backends.name: olmOCR
backends.price_note: Free, open-source (Apache-2.0). No license/API fee. Self-hosted compute cost only: Ai2 reports ~$190-200 per 1,000,000 PDF pages (roughly $0.0002/page; "10,000 pages for less than $2" on a single H100 with FP8), about 1/32 the cost of GPT-4o batch API. As-of 2026-06. GPU rental/electricity is the real cost driver; there is no official hosted endpoint.
backends.free_tier: Entirely free — code (GitHub) and weights (Hugging Face) are Apache-2.0; only your own GPU/compute is required.
backends.python_install: pip install olmocr[gpu] --extra-index-url https://download.pytorch.org/whl/cu128
backends.accuracy_note: olmOCR-Bench (the project's own 1,400+ doc / 7,000+ test-case benchmark): olmOCR-2-7B-1025 scores 82.4 +/- 1.1 overall (model card lists 82.3 +/- 1.1), a near-SOTA open result. Category scores: Base 99.7, Headers/Footers 95.7, Math ~82-84, Multi-column ~84, ArXiv 82.9, Long-tiny-text 81.4, Tables ~48-85 (figures vary by report). Beats Marker (76.1) and MinerU (75.8) on the same bench. Tables remain the weakest category. No standardized OmniDocBench or OCRBench number is published by Ai2 for olmOCR-2 as of 2026-06; comparisons are on olmOCR-Bench. (Source: Ai2 olmOCR-2 blog and HF model card.)
backends.languages_note: Officially English-only. The Qwen2.5-VL-7B backbone is multilingual (Latin, CJK, Arabic, Cyrillic, etc.), but olmOCR's training mix (olmOCR-mix-1025) was filtered to English, so non-English documents may work informally but are unsupported and degraded. For broad multilingual OCR, alternatives like PaddleOCR-VL or DeepSeek-OCR (~100+ languages) are better suited.
backends.best_for: Large-scale, cost-efficient linearization of English PDFs (academic papers, historical scans, legal docs, multi-column reports, math/tables) into clean Markdown for LLM/RAG training corpora and document pipelines — when you have GPUs and want full local control and an open license.
pros: Near-SOTA open accuracy on olmOCR-Bench (82.4) — beats Marker and MinerU, strong on math, multi-column, headers/footer removal, and natural reading order
Fully open and permissive: Apache-2.0 code AND weights, on-prem, no data leaves your machine, no vendor lock-in
Very low marginal cost at scale (~$190-200 per million pages) and designed for high-throughput vLLM/SGLang batch inference scaling from 1 to hundreds of GPUs
Runs on modest hardware (12 GB VRAM minimum; RTX 4090 works) with FP8 and GGUF/Ollama/LM Studio quantized variants for accessibility
Clean Markdown output with equations, tables, and multi-column handling; good fit for LLM training/RAG pipelines
cons: English-only officially — non-English / CJK / Arabic documents are unsupported and unreliable
Requires an NVIDIA GPU; no official hosted API/SaaS, so you operate the inference stack yourself
Tables are the weakest benchmark category and complex tables can degrade
VLM-based, so subject to hallucination/omission risks and slower per-page than classic OCR engines; no bounding boxes or per-token confidence scores
Setup overhead (vLLM/SGLang, CUDA, ~30 GB disk) is heavier than drop-in libraries; best value only realized at batch scale
backends.speed_note: Throughput-optimized for batch via vLLM/SGLang; ~10,000 pages for under $2 on a single H100 (FP8), scaling near-linearly to hundreds of GPUs and S3/Beaker multi-node clusters. Per-page latency is higher than classic OCR (it's a 7B VLM), so it shines on large batches, not single low-latency requests.
backends.privacy_note: Fully local / on-prem — model runs on your own GPU and no data leaves the machine. No telemetry or cloud dependency. A remote vLLM-server mode exists but points at infrastructure you control. Ideal for sensitive/regulated corpora.
backends.maturity_note: Active and popular: ~17.4k GitHub stars, 1.4k forks; olmOCR-2 (v0.4.0) released 2025-10-22, latest pipeline release v0.4.27 (2026-03-12); current model allenai/olmOCR-2-7B-1025 with FP8 and 11 quantized community variants. Backed by Ai2 with a published paper (arXiv:2510.19817). As-of 2026-06.

backends.name: OnnxTR
backends.vendor: Felix Dittrich (felixdittrich92), open-source community; builds on Mindee docTR
backends.price_note: Free and open-source (Apache-2.0). No license fee, no API/usage cost — runs entirely on your own CPU/GPU. Pretrained ONNX weights are downloaded free from the Hugging Face Hub. Only cost is your own compute. As of 2026-06.
backends.free_tier: Fully free; unlimited local use. No paid tier exists.
backends.python_install: pip install "onnxtr[cpu]"  (GPU: pip install "onnxtr[gpu]"; Intel: pip install "onnxtr[openvino]"; headless variants e.g. onnxtr[cpu-headless])
backends.accuracy_note: No OnnxTR-specific accuracy benchmark is published; OnnxTR reuses the exact docTR model weights (converted to ONNX), so accuracy equals docTR's. docTR's published end-to-end (detection+recognition) exact-match scores: F1 ~87% on FUNSD and ~95% on CORD (default db_resnet50 + crnn_vgg16_bn pipeline, per docTR docs). 8-bit quantized ONNX variants trade a small accuracy drop for speed. No OmniDocBench/OCRBench entry found for OnnxTR specifically. (as of 2026-06)
backends.speed_note: Fast for a non-LLM engine. Per OnnxTR's own README benchmarks (v0.6.0): CPU i7-14700K full precision ~0.57s/page (FUNSD), 8-bit ~0.38s, OpenVINO ~0.15s; smallest model combo (db_mobilenet_v3_large + crnn_mobilenet_v3_small) ~0.17s/page. GPU RTX 4080 ~0.06s/page (float16 ~0.05s). Lighter dependency footprint and lower latency than framework-based docTR.
backends.languages_note: Default models are English/Latin-trained. A multilingual PARSeq model (parseq_multilingual_v1, from docTR) covers 14 Latin-script European languages: English, French, German, Italian, Spanish, Portuguese, Czech, Polish, Dutch, Norwegian, Danish, Finnish, Swedish. No native CJK, Arabic, Cyrillic, or Indic support out of the box (would require custom-trained recognition models with a matching vocab). Recognition vocab is swappable.
backends.best_for: Production OCR on printed/scanned documents where you want docTR's quality but a lightweight, TensorFlow/PyTorch-free install with fast CPU inference (8-bit quantization, OpenVINO) or simple GPU/CoreML deployment — e.g. embedding OCR in containers, edge/CPU servers, or as a Docling OCR backend.
pros: No TensorFlow or PyTorch dependency — small install, fast cold start, easy to containerize; runs on plain ONNX Runtime
Multiple execution providers out of the box: CPU, CUDA (NVIDIA), OpenVINO (Intel CPU/GPU), CoreML (Apple Silicon)
8-bit quantized and float16 model variants for substantially faster CPU/GPU inference with minimal code change
Reuses docTR's full model zoo (DBNet/LinkNet/FAST detection; CRNN/SAR/MASTER/ViTSTR/PARSeq/VIPTR recognition) with word-level bounding boxes and confidence scores
Fully free, permissive Apache-2.0, fully local/offline — no data leaves the machine, good for privacy/regulated use
Drop-in API mirroring docTR plus exports to JSON, plain text, and hOCR; ships a Docling OCR plugin
cons: English/Latin-only in practice; multilingual model covers just 14 European languages, no CJK/Arabic/Cyrillic/Indic without custom training
No higher-level document understanding: no native table extraction, math/formula, key-value, charts, or handwriting support
Smaller project (~180 GitHub stars) maintained largely by one author — less ecosystem/community than Tesseract, PaddleOCR, or commercial APIs
Accuracy is capped by docTR's models; not competitive with modern VLM/LLM OCR on complex or degraded layouts
Reading-order/layout structure is limited (word boxes + simple page assembly), not a full layout-analysis engine
GPU path requires correct CUDA/cuDNN setup; quantized models trade some accuracy for speed
backends.privacy_note: Fully local/offline inference — no data leaves the machine. Pretrained weights are fetched once from the Hugging Face Hub (can be pre-downloaded/cached for air-gapped use). On-prem by default; no telemetry or cloud calls during OCR.
backends.maturity_note: Active single-maintainer project. ~180 GitHub stars; latest release v0.8.1 on 2026-02-04. Tracks docTR closely and ships a Docling OCR plugin (docling-OCR-OnnxTR). Regular releases; Python 3.10+. (as of 2026-06)

backends.free_tier: Entirely free as software with unlimited local OCR. Cloud-engine free tiers depend on the chosen provider (e.g. OCRSpace free key; Google/Azure monthly free quotas on the user's own account).

backends.accuracy_note: No standardized benchmark (OmniDocBench/OCRBench/CER/WER) is published for owocr itself; as an aggregator its accuracy equals that of the chosen backend. Maintainer's qualitative ranking (README, as of 2026-06): Google Lens "arguably the best OCR engine to date", Bing a "close second", Chrome Screen AI "possibly the best local engine to date"; OneOCR and meikiocr rated comparable and strong for Japanese; NDLOCR-Lite suited to documents/book scans. beyond_text: handwriting (only via backends that support it, e.g. Apple Vision / cloud engines)
backends.speed_note: Designed for low-latency interactive use (continuous screen/clipboard scanning). A two-pass system sends only changed screen regions to an online engine, combining local speed with cloud accuracy and reducing API calls. Local-only engines (Apple Vision, WinRT OCR, OneOCR, Chrome Screen AI) give near-instant per-image results; EasyOCR/RapidOCR/meikiocr are faster with a GPU. Cloud engines add network round-trip latency.
backends.privacy_note: Fully on-device when using local engines (Apple Vision/Live Text, WinRT OCR, OneOCR, Chrome Screen AI, EasyOCR, RapidOCR, Manga OCR, meikiocr, NDLOCR-Lite) — no data leaves the machine. Cloud engines (Google Lens, Bing, Google Vision, Azure Document Intelligence, OCRSpace) transmit image regions to third-party servers. Because owocr lets you pick the backend, it can be run entirely offline/on-prem.
backends.maturity_note: Active single-maintainer project. PyPI latest 1.26.8 (released 28 March, recent; 100+ releases in version history through late 2025). GitHub ~258 stars as of 2026-06. Requires Python >=3.11. Frequent small releases indicate ongoing maintenance.
backends.best_for: Real-time, on-screen Japanese text capture for language learning, manga, visual novels, and anime — and more broadly as a single Python/CLI facade that unifies native OS OCR (Apple Vision, Windows OCR/OneOCR), local libraries (EasyOCR, RapidOCR, Manga OCR), and cloud engines (Google Lens/Vision, Bing, Azure, OCRSpace) behind one interface.

backends.best_for: High-accuracy multilingual document parsing and OCR where you want full control and zero per-page fees: self-hosted pipelines for printed/scene/handwritten text, tables, formulas and charts, with a choice between an ultra-lightweight CPU/edge pipeline (PP-OCRv5/v6) and a SOTA VLM (PaddleOCR-VL) for complex documents and LLM ingestion.

Broad coverage: 100+/109 languages and rich beyond-text capabilities (tables, formulas/math, charts, handwriting, layout and reading order) with Markdown/JSON/DOCX output for LLM pipelines

backends.name: pix2tex / LaTeX-OCR
backends.price_note: Free and open source (MIT). No usage fees, no API costs. Pretrained model checkpoints download automatically on first run. Only cost is your own compute. As of 2026-06.
backends.free_tier: Fully free — entire package and pretrained weights are free under MIT with no quota.
backends.python_install: pip install "pix2tex[gui]"  (extras: [api], [train]; bare `pip install pix2tex` for the Python/CLI API only)
backends.accuracy_note: Self-reported metrics on the project's held-out test set (README/docs): BLEU 0.88, normalized edit distance 0.10, token accuracy 0.60. These are math-formula-specific, not whole-document OCR. No OmniDocBench/OCRBench whole-page scores apply (it is not a page OCR engine). Third-party math-OCR papers (e.g. Texify, Pix2Text MFR, UniMERNet) routinely use pix2tex as a baseline and report it being outperformed by newer transformer models on complex/long expressions and handwriting; on simple printed equations it remains competitive.
backends.languages_note: Not a natural-language OCR engine — it recognizes the LaTeX math markup language, not human languages. Input is mathematical notation (Latin letters, Greek symbols, operators, and standard math constructs as rendered by LaTeX). No multilingual text-script support (no CJK/Arabic/Cyrillic prose); surrounding natural-language text is out of scope.
backends.best_for: Turning images/screenshots of a single printed mathematical equation into LaTeX, locally and for free — e.g. capturing formulas from PDFs/papers/websites into editable LaTeX via the screenshot GUI or batch via the Python API.
backends.speed_note: Single-equation inference is fast: typically sub-second on a GPU and a few seconds per image on CPU. Lightweight model (ViT+ResNet encoder, small Transformer decoder), so it runs comfortably on modest hardware; CPU-only is fully usable.
backends.privacy_note: Runs entirely on-device. No data leaves the machine — there is no cloud API. Pretrained weights are downloaded once from the project's release assets, after which it works fully offline. Good fit for sensitive/air-gapped use.
backends.maturity_note: Mature and widely used; ~16.5k GitHub stars (as of 2026-06). Latest PyPI release pix2tex 0.1.4 dated 2025-01-18. Development has slowed — maintenance/minor fixes rather than active feature work — but it remains the de facto open-source baseline for math-to-LaTeX OCR and is broadly cited.
pros: Free, MIT-licensed, fully local/offline after a one-time weight download — no API keys, no per-page cost, strong privacy
Purpose-built for math: produces clean LaTeX for printed equations with good accuracy (BLEU ~0.88, norm. edit distance ~0.10)
Multiple ready interfaces out of the box: Python API (`LatexOCR`), CLI, a screenshot/snipping GUI (`latexocr`), and a Streamlit/REST API server (Docker image available)
Lightweight and CPU-friendly — runs without a GPU and on modest hardware
Mature, widely adopted (~16.5k stars), well documented, and the standard open-source baseline for formula OCR
cons: Math-only and single-equation oriented — does not do page layout, plain-text paragraphs, tables, or document structure; needs the equation cropped/isolated
Handwriting support is experimental and weak; trained mostly on computer-generated formulas, so it struggles with handwritten or noisy input
Accuracy degrades on long/complex multi-line expressions and matrices; newer models (Texify, UniMERNet, Pix2Text MFR) outperform it on hard cases
No bounding boxes, no confidence scores, single output format (LaTeX only — no MathML/SVG)
Development has largely stalled (last release Jan 2025); no roadmap for multilingual text or document-level OCR

backends.name: RapidOCR
backends.price_note: Free and open-source (Apache-2.0). No usage fees, no API, no subscription. Only cost is your own compute. As of June 2026.

Independent comparison surveys note PaddleOCR/RapidOCR offer "the best trade-off between accuracy, speed and memory efficiency" among open-source OCR and are the most memory-efficient options (Nanonets OCR API benchmark, 2025). Treat as: no standardized RapidOCR-specific benchmark found; inherits PP-OCR/PP-OCRv4/v5 accuracy.
backends.speed_note: Optimized for fast offline CPU inference; "extreme speed" is a stated core advantage. ONNX Runtime CPU is the default; onnxruntime-gpu (CUDA) and PaddlePaddle-GPU available for acceleration. Community reports ~150ms/image with ONNXRuntime CUDA GPU acceleration. Mobile model variants run on resource-constrained / edge devices.
backends.languages_note: ~12 recognition language/script models (mirroring PaddleOCR): Simplified Chinese (ch), English (en), Traditional Chinese (chinese_cht), Japanese (japan), Korean (korean), Latin (Romance/Germanic), Cyrillic (Russian/Bulgarian/etc.), Arabic, Devanagari (Hindi/Sanskrit), Kannada, Tamil, Telugu. Default models cover Chinese + English. Text detection has 3 options (ch, en, multi). The Latin/Cyrillic/Arabic/Devanagari multilingual models cover 80+ underlying languages via PaddleOCR character dictionaries. Scripts: Latin, CJK (Chinese/Japanese/Korean), Cyrillic, Arabic, Indic (Devanagari/Kannada/Tamil/Telugu).
backends.best_for: Fast, fully offline, privacy-preserving multilingual OCR (especially Chinese/CJK + English) embedded into applications across Python, C++, Java, C#, Android, iOS, and .NET without a Python/Paddle dependency. Ideal when you want PaddleOCR's accuracy but need lightweight ONNX Runtime deployment, edge/mobile inference, or non-Python integration.
pros: Apache-2.0, completely free, runs 100% offline/on-device — no data leaves the machine, strong privacy
Ships pre-converted PaddleOCR (PP-OCR) models to ONNX, so you get PaddleOCR-level accuracy without installing PaddlePaddle
Genuinely cross-platform and polyglot: Python, C++, Java, C#, .NET, Android, iOS bindings from one model set
Pluggable inference backends (ONNX Runtime, OpenVINO, MNN, PaddlePaddle, TensorRT, PyTorch) let you tune for CPU/GPU/edge
Lightweight and memory-efficient with mobile model variants for constrained devices; fast offline CPU inference

backends.name: Microsoft Table Transformer (TATR)
backends.price_note: Free and open-source (MIT). No service/API fees; you run the models yourself, so the only cost is your own compute/GPU. Model weights download free from Hugging Face. As of 2026-06.
backends.free_tier: Fully free: all code (MIT) and pre-trained weights are downloadable at no cost, with no usage limits beyond your own hardware.
backends.python_install: pip install transformers timm torch torchvision pillow (Hugging Face route); or clone the repo and use the provided conda environment.yml. For a full PDF pipeline also add pdf2image/pytesseract for image conversion and text extraction.
backends.privacy_note: Fully local/on-premise: documents never leave your machine. No telemetry or cloud calls; weights and code are downloaded once and run offline thereafter. Suitable for sensitive/regulated documents.
backends.accuracy_note: Strong on table-structure benchmarks (not OCR text CER/WER). On PubTables-1M, TATR-v1.0 structure recognition: AP 0.902, GriTS-Top 0.9849, GriTS-Con 0.9850, GriTS-Loc 0.9786, cell-content accuracy 0.8243; detection AP50 0.995 / AP 0.970. On the cross-dataset ICDAR-2013 exact-match benchmark (v1.1 "Aligning benchmark datasets" paper, ICDAR 2023), TATR improved after dataset alignment from 65%/42%/69% to 75%/65%/81% for PubTables-1M / FinTabNet / combined training. TATR does not transcribe text itself, so OmniDocBench/OCRBench CER/WER do not directly apply; no standardized OCR text-accuracy benchmark found for it.
backends.languages_note: No documented language list. TATR detects table geometry (rows/columns/cells/headers), not text, so it is largely script-agnostic for layout. Models were trained on predominantly English scientific (PubTables-1M) and financial (FinTabNet) documents; text content must be supplied by a separate OCR/PDF text-extraction step, where language coverage depends on that tool.
backends.best_for: Detecting tables and recovering their cell/row/column structure from PDFs and document images (especially scientific and financial reports), as a specialized stage in a document-extraction pipeline rather than a general OCR engine.
backends.speed_note: Lightweight DETR models (~28.8M params, 110 MB each) run fast on a GPU and are usable on CPU for low volume. Two-stage pipeline (detection then structure recognition per cropped table) adds overhead; throughput scales with GPU.
backends.maturity_note: Mature and widely used but in maintenance mode. ~2.9k GitHub stars, ~310 forks; last tagged release v1.0.0 (Feb 2023), ~195 commits. HF weights see very heavy usage (table-transformer-detection ~1.8M downloads/month, structure-recognition ~1.4M/month as of 2026-06). Microsoft Research recently published a successor dataset (PubTables-v2, arXiv Dec 2025).
pros: Free, MIT-licensed, and fully self-hostable with no API keys or per-page fees
Excellent table detection and cell-structure (GriTS) accuracy on document/financial layouts
First-class Hugging Face transformers integration; trivial to load via pipeline('object-detection', ...)
Runs fully offline/on-prem, good for sensitive documents; CPU-capable, small models (~110 MB)
Ships the open PubTables-1M dataset and the GriTS evaluation metric for reproducible benchmarking
cons: Not a full OCR engine: it only finds tables and their structure; you must add a separate OCR/PDF text-extraction step to get cell text
Scope limited to tables; no general text, math, handwriting, barcodes, or charts
Two-stage detection+structure pipeline requires non-trivial glue code (cropping, padding, OCR alignment) to produce final HTML/CSV
Training data skews English scientific/financial; may degrade on complex, rotated, borderless, or non-English/CJK tables
Repo is in maintenance mode (last release Feb 2023); limited ongoing development

backends.name: Tabula / tabula-py
backends.vendor: chezou (Aki Ariga) / Tabula project (ProPublica, Knight Foundation)
backends.price_note: Free and open source (MIT). No usage fees, no API, no quotas. As of 2026-06. Only "cost" is a local JVM (Java 8+) install.
backends.free_tier: Fully free; runs entirely locally with no account or API key.
backends.python_install: pip install tabula-py (requires Java 8+ on PATH; optional: pip install "tabula-py[jpype]" for faster JVM bridge)
backends.accuracy_note: No standardized OCR benchmark applies — tabula-py is PDF-native table extraction, not image OCR, so it does not appear in OmniDocBench/OCRBench/CER/WER leaderboards. Accuracy depends entirely on table type and chosen mode. In an informal Camelot-wiki comparison (10 lattice + 10 stream PDFs), Camelot outperformed Tabula on lattice (ruled) tables, while Tabula did better table *detection* on stream (whitespace) tables but produced weaker parsing output. No published CER/WER figures exist; quality is high on clean text-based PDFs and degrades on merged cells, multi-line cells, and irregular layouts.
backends.languages_note: Not an OCR/script-recognition tool — it reads the embedded text layer of a PDF, so it is effectively language- and script-agnostic for any text the PDF already encodes (Latin, CJK, Arabic, Cyrillic, Indic, etc.). Known caveat: encoding/garbling issues (e.g. "?" characters) reported on Windows; non-Latin scripts may need correct pandas encoding options.
backends.best_for: Extracting tabular data from text-based (digitally generated) PDFs into pandas DataFrames or CSV/TSV/JSON — financial reports, government data dumps, scientific tables — in a scripted Python pipeline, free and on-prem.
pros: Free, MIT-licensed, fully local — no API, no key, no data leaves the machine; ideal for sensitive/regulated documents

backends.name: Tesseract (pytesseract / tesserocr)
backends.vendor: tesseract-ocr community (originally HP; sponsored by Google 2006-2018; maintained by Zdenko Podobny, Stefan Weil et al.)
backends.self_hostable_note: Runs entirely on-device; no network calls. The de-facto self-hosted OCR baseline.
backends.price_note: Free and open source (Apache-2.0). No usage fees, no API costs, no quotas. As of 2026-06, the only cost is your own compute. Python wrappers (pytesseract, tesserocr) are also free/OSS.
backends.free_tier: Unlimited — fully free OSS, run locally at no cost.
backends.python_install: pip install pytesseract  (subprocess wrapper; requires the `tesseract` binary installed separately) OR pip install tesserocr  (Cython C++ binding; requires libtesseract-dev + libleptonica-dev)
backends.accuracy_note: No single standardized benchmark is published by the project. On clean printed text Tesseract (LSTM engine) reaches ~98-99% character accuracy (comparable to ABBYY FineReader per AIMultiple). On noisier real-world data it degrades: an independent receipt-OCR study reports CER ~15.6% and WER ~30.8% for Tesseract. It is consistently outperformed on document benchmarks (e.g. OmniDocBench) by newer engines like PaddleOCR (PP-OCRv5 ~94.5% on OmniDocBench v1.5) and VLM-based OCR. Accuracy is highly sensitive to preprocessing (x-height >=20px, deskew, binarization, border removal). Sources: AIMultiple OCR accuracy study; Modal OCR comparison; arXiv ReceiptSense 2406.04493.
backends.languages_note: Wikipedia documents 116 languages across 37 scripts for the v4+ LSTM models; the project README and distro packages advertise "100+" (Linux distros ship 130+ traineddata files / 35+ scripts). Broad script coverage: Latin, CJK (Chinese simplified/traditional, Japanese, Korean), Arabic, Cyrillic, Hebrew, Greek, Armenian, Georgian, and Indic scripts (Devanagari/Hindi, Bengali, Tamil, Telugu, Kannada, Gujarati, etc.), plus Thai, Khmer, Lao, Burmese, Cherokee, and more. Three model qualities per language: fast (int), best (float), and standard.
backends.speed_note: CPU-only engine (no GPU support). Fast on clean single-column printed text, especially with the `fast` integer models. tesserocr runs in-process and releases the GIL during recognition, enabling real multi-threaded concurrency; pytesseract spawns a subprocess per call (higher overhead for batch/many-small-image workloads). Slower than GPU-accelerated modern OCR on large documents.
backends.privacy_note: Fully local/on-premise — image data never leaves the machine, no network calls. Ideal for sensitive/offline/air-gapped use. No telemetry.
backends.maturity_note: Very mature and actively maintained. Core repo ~74.8k GitHub stars; latest stable Tesseract 5.5.2 (2025-12-26). pytesseract 0.3.13 (2024-08-16). tesserocr 2.10.0 (2026-01-13, ~2.2k stars). Origins at HP (1985-1994), open-sourced 2005, Google-sponsored 2006-2018. As-of 2026-06.
backends.best_for: Local, free, offline OCR of clean printed/typed documents in many languages where data privacy or zero cost matters. A solid baseline/default for digitizing books, scanned PDFs, and forms; good when you control preprocessing. Not the right tool for handwriting, math, complex multi-column layouts, or table-structure extraction.

backends.name: TrOCR
backends.price_note: Free and open-source (model weights + Transformers library). No usage fees. As of 2026-06, the only cost is your own compute (CPU/GPU). Weights and code are MIT-licensed via the microsoft/unilm repo and Hugging Face Hub.
backends.free_tier: Fully free; unlimited local use under MIT license.
backends.python_install: pip install transformers torch pillow (optionally: accelerate, bitsandbytes for quantization)
backends.accuracy_note: On the IAM handwriting benchmark, TrOCR-Large achieves CER 2.89% and TrOCR-Base CER 3.42% (vs >7% for older CNN-RNN approaches). On the SROIE printed-receipt benchmark it reaches F1 96.60 (Large), 96.34 (Base), 95.86 (Small). These are line-level recognition scores from the original paper (Li et al., 2021, arXiv:2109.10282); the paper reported state-of-the-art on printed, handwritten, and scene-text line recognition at publication. No OmniDocBench/OCRBench scores apply since TrOCR is a line-recognition model, not a full-page document parser.
backends.languages_note: Official Microsoft checkpoints are English-only (Latin script), trained on IAM (handwritten) and SROIE (printed). No official multilingual checkpoint has been released. The architecture supports other languages via the XLM-RoBERTa tokenizer, and the community has fine-tuned it for other languages/scripts (e.g. Spanish TrOCR, Chinese, Korean Hanja), but each requires a separately trained checkpoint. Out of the box: English/Latin only.
backends.best_for: Recognizing the text content of pre-cropped single text-line images (printed or handwritten), especially English documents where you already have a line/word detector and want high-accuracy transformer-based recognition that runs fully offline.
pros: Strong line-level accuracy: SOTA-level CER on IAM handwriting (2.89% Large) and ~96 F1 on SROIE printed receipts at release
Dedicated handwritten checkpoints (base/large-handwritten) make it one of the best off-the-shelf handwriting recognizers
Fully local, MIT-licensed, no API keys, no per-page cost, data never leaves the machine
Trivial to run via Hugging Face Transformers (TrOCRProcessor + VisionEncoderDecoderModel, ~8 lines); 8-bit quantization supported
Easy to fine-tune for new domains/languages/scripts (XLM-RoBERTa tokenizer; published Colab fine-tuning notebooks)
cons: Recognition-only: no text detection/localization. You must supply pre-cropped single text-line images yourself
No layout analysis, reading order, tables, math, or bounding boxes; not a full-page document OCR system
Multi-line input causes hallucination/degradation; one model call per line means slow throughput on dense documents
Official checkpoints are English/Latin only; other languages need a separately fine-tuned model
Autoregressive decoding is relatively slow vs CTC-style recognizers, especially on CPU; large checkpoint (~0.3B+) benefits from a GPU
No native confidence scores or word-level boxes returned
backends.speed_note: Autoregressive seq2seq decoding makes it slower per image than CTC-based recognizers; one forward+generate pass per text line. Practical on CPU for a few lines, but a GPU is recommended for batches or full pages. Base ~0.3B params; small/large variants trade speed for accuracy. 8-bit (bitsandbytes) quantization available to reduce memory.
backends.privacy_note: Runs entirely on your own hardware; no data leaves the machine. Self-hostable and air-gappable once weights are downloaded.
backends.maturity_note: Published by Microsoft Research (paper arXiv:2109.10282, AAAI 2022); integrated into Hugging Face Transformers and actively maintained there (model_doc current through Transformers v5.12.0 as of 2026-06). Part of the well-established microsoft/unilm repo (tens of thousands of GitHub stars). Core checkpoints (small/base/large x printed/handwritten/stage1) are stable and widely used; microsoft/trocr-base-printed has 24+ community fine-tunes. Mature and stable rather than rapidly evolving.

backends.name: TrOCR (handwritten)
backends.vendor: Microsoft Research (UniLM); distributed via Hugging Face
backends.price_note: Free, open-source model weights (MIT license). No usage fees. Cost is only your own compute/GPU. If served behind the Hugging Face Inference Providers/Endpoints, you pay that platform's compute rates, but the model itself is free.
backends.free_tier: Entirely free; self-host the weights with no API key required.
backends.python_install: pip install transformers torch pillow
backends.accuracy_note: On the IAM Handwriting Database test set (English, single text lines), the original TrOCR paper (Li et al., 2021, arXiv:2109.10282) and the microsoft/unilm repo report cased CER of ~2.89% for TrOCR-Large-Handwritten and ~3.42% for TrOCR-Base-Handwritten; this was state-of-the-art on IAM at publication. Independent reproductions report ~2.6-3.4% CER on IAM. No OmniDocBench/OCRBench scores apply because TrOCR is a single-line recognizer, not a full-document/layout engine; those benchmarks target full-page document OCR. Caveat: accuracy degrades sharply outside the IAM domain (non-English, heavily degraded scans, multi-line/full-page input without external line segmentation).
backends.speed_note: Autoregressive decoding makes it slower than CTC-based recognizers; large checkpoint is notably heavier. Practical throughput is a few to tens of lines/sec on a modern GPU (batched), and much slower on CPU. The small checkpoint and 8-bit quantization (bitsandbytes) reduce latency/memory. Throughput is per text-line, so a full page requires an external line/word segmentation step first, multiplying total time.
backends.languages_note: English / Latin script only for the official handwritten checkpoints, fine-tuned on the IAM English handwriting database. No official multilingual handwritten checkpoint from Microsoft. The decoder is RoBERTa-based (English); community-trained variants exist for other languages (e.g. via XLM-RoBERTa decoder) but are third-party, not part of the official model.
backends.maturity_note: Mature and widely used. Part of Microsoft's UniLM project; transformers integration contributed by nielsr. As of 2026-06 the handwritten checkpoints remain popular on Hugging Face (trocr-large-handwritten ~282k downloads/month, trocr-base-handwritten ~125k/month, trocr-small-handwritten ~370k/month). Model is stable but not actively iterated (no successor handwritten checkpoint from Microsoft; all three handwritten checkpoints last modified 2024-05-27). Still works with current transformers v5.x via VisionEncoderDecoderModel + TrOCRProcessor (direct loading), BUT note: the legacy 'image-to-text' pipeline was REMOVED in transformers v5 — you must load the model directly or pin transformers<5.0.0 to use that pipeline.
backends.privacy_note: Fully local / on-prem. Weights run on your own hardware; no data leaves the machine. No API call or telemetry at inference time once weights are downloaded.
backends.best_for: High-accuracy recognition of English handwritten (cursive included) single text-line images when you already have line/word segmentation and want a free, self-hostable, MIT-licensed model. Ideal as the recognition stage in a custom handwriting pipeline (e.g. after a detector like CRAFT or a layout/line segmenter).
pros: Free, open-source (MIT) and fully self-hostable — no API keys, no per-page cost, data stays on-prem
Strong accuracy on English handwriting, including cursive (~2.89% CER on IAM for the large checkpoint), SOTA at publication

English/Latin only in official checkpoints; no official multilingual handwritten model
No layout, tables, math, bounding boxes, reading order, or confidence scores in the output — plain text only

backends.python_install: pip install google-genai
backends.accuracy_note: Strong OCR benchmark results (community/third-party, since Google's own docs don't publish CER/WER). On OmniDocBench v1.5 (overall edit distance, lower=better): Gemini 3 Pro ~0.115, Gemini 2.5 Pro ~0.145 (tied with Claude Sonnet 4.5; ahead of GPT-5.1 ~0.147). Note: OmniDocBench is increasingly considered saturated, and some small specialist OCR models (e.g. GLM-OCR 0.9B at ~94.62 on OmniDocBench v1.5) now reportedly exceed Gemini 3 Pro on pure document-parsing edit distance. Accuracy depends heavily on using media_resolution/vision setting HIGH for small/dense text.
backends.languages_note: Officially documents ~37 fully supported languages (Latin, CJK — Chinese simplified/traditional, Japanese, Korean — Cyrillic, Greek, Hebrew, Arabic, Indic such as Hindi/Bengali, Thai, Vietnamese, Indonesian, Swahili, etc.). Certain models (e.g. Gemini 1.5/2.0 Flash) extend to additional languages (Amharic, Persian, Azerbaijani, Welsh, Basque, etc.). In practice the underlying multimodal models read far more scripts than the 37 'supported' for text generation; OCR works across most printed Latin/CJK/Cyrillic/Arabic/Indic scripts.
backends.maturity_note: Mature, heavily-used flagship product from Google, actively maintained and production-grade with a large developer ecosystem (google-genai SDK, v2.x, updated continuously through 2026). As of 2026-06 the live API centers on Gemini 2.5 (Pro/Flash/Flash-Lite) and current-generation Gemini 3.x / 3.5 families (e.g. Gemini 3.5 Flash stable, Gemini 3.1 Pro Preview, Gemini 3.1 Flash-Lite). Note: the older generations in this option's name are no longer callable -- Gemini 1.5 models are fully shut down (requests return 404) and Gemini 2.0 Flash / Flash-Lite were shut down on 2026-06-01; Gemini 2.5 models carry a retirement date around 2026-10-16. New model versions ship every few months and older ones are deprecated and retired on a rolling schedule, so pin to a current model id (e.g. gemini-2.5-flash or gemini-3.5-flash) and check the deprecations page.
backends.speed_note: Latency-tier dependent: Flash/Flash-Lite models are fast and cheap for high-volume OCR; Pro models are slower but more accurate. Per-page round-trip is API-bound (network + token generation), typically a few seconds per page; throughput is gated by free/paid rate limits (RPM/TPM/RPD) rather than local compute. Batch API trades latency for ~50% cost reduction.
backends.privacy_note: Cloud-only; image/PDF data is sent to Google servers. On the PAID tier, Google states data is not used to train models. On the FREE tier, prompts/responses MAY be used to improve Google products/models — do not send sensitive documents on the free tier. No on-prem option via Gemini API; enterprise data-governance options exist via Vertex AI (Google Cloud) with stronger contractual data controls.
pros: Top-tier OCR accuracy on document benchmarks (OmniDocBench ~0.115-0.145 edit distance; OCRBench ~83-88%), with strong handwriting, math/LaTeX, table, and chart-to-structured-data ('derendering' to HTML/LaTeX/Markdown) support
Native long-context PDF ingestion up to 1000 pages / 50MB per file via the Files API — no separate OCR preprocessing or page-splitting pipeline needed

Prompt-steerable: you ask in natural language for Markdown, JSON, key-value extraction, translation, or bounding boxes ([0-1000] normalized coords) in one call, combining OCR with reasoning/extraction
Generous no-card free tier for prototyping and low-volume use; cheap Flash/Flash-Lite tiers plus ~50% batch discount make high-volume OCR cost-competitive
Broad language/script coverage (~37 documented, many more in practice) and trivial integration (REST + google-genai SDK)
cons: Cloud/API-only with closed weights — documents leave your machine; free-tier prompts may be used for training, so unsuitable for sensitive data without the paid/Vertex AI path

Token-billed and non-deterministic LLM output: cost scales with image/page count and it can hallucinate, omit, or 'correct' text rather than transcribe verbatim — risky for high-fidelity OCR without validation
No native per-character/per-word confidence scores and no built-in hOCR/ALTO output; bounding boxes are prompt-elicited and less precise/reliable than dedicated OCR engines
Requires HIGH media_resolution setting for small/dense text or accuracy drops; defaults favor cost over OCR fidelity
Frequent model churn and deprecations (1.5 -> 2.x -> 3.x) mean pinning/migration overhead; rate limits (RPM/TPM/RPD) can throttle batch OCR workloads
Specialist open-source OCR models now match or beat it on pure document-parsing edit distance at far lower cost, so it's overkill when you only need plain transcription
backends.best_for: Teams that want one API to do OCR plus understanding — extracting structured data (tables, key-value, JSON), transcribing handwriting/historical documents, reading math/charts, or converting PDFs to Markdown/LaTeX — over long multi-page documents, without standing up local infrastructure, and who can accept cloud processing and LLM non-determinism.

backends.price_note: As of 2026-06: DOCUMENT_TEXT_DETECTION is billed at $1.50 per 1,000 units (images/pages) for units 1,001–5,000,000/month, and $0.60 per 1,000 units beyond 5,000,000/month. backends.free_tier: First 1,000 units/month free (per feature). No perpetual free unlimited tier; new GCP accounts may also have general signup credits, but Vision itself is free only up to the 1,000 units/month allowance.
backends.python_install: pip install google-cloud-vision
backends.api_env_var: GOOGLE_APPLICATION_CREDENTIALS (service-account JSON for Application Default Credentials)
backends.self_hostable_note: Not self-hostable. Google Cloud-only managed API. (No on-prem/offline deployment of this model.)
backends.accuracy_note: No standardized OmniDocBench/OCRBench figure published by Google for this specific feature. Third-party benchmarks: AIMultiple (May 2021, cosine-similarity over a mixed dataset) reports ~98.0% overall accuracy, ~99.1–99.2% on printed English; handwriting is notably lower. A January 2026 AIMultiple refresh reports ~95% on printed text / ~85% on printed media (different methodology). Printed/dense-document OCR is industry-leading; handwriting is usable but materially weaker than printed text. Treat all third-party numbers as indicative, not official.
backends.languages_note: No single official total; docs list ~100+ supported, ~70+ experimental, and ~150+ mapped language variants (~320+ total entries). Scripts: Latin, Cyrillic, CJK (Chinese/Japanese/Korean), Arabic/Persian/Urdu, Indic (Hindi, Bengali, Tamil, Telugu, Kannada, Malayalam, Gujarati, Punjabi, Marathi, Nepali, Oriya, Assamese), Greek, Hebrew, Thai, Khmer, Lao, Myanmar, Georgian, Armenian, Syriac, Tibetan, Ethiopic. DOCUMENT_TEXT_DETECTION auto-detects the full supported set (TEXT_DETECTION only a subset). Handwriting recognition is limited to a narrow set of scripts: Latin, Japanese, Korean, plus experimental Bengali, Cyrillic, Devanagari, and Greek; English handwriting can be hinted via language code "en-t-i0-handwrit".

backends.name: LlamaParse
backends.price_note: As of 2026-06: credit-based, 1,000 credits = $1.25 (same in North America and Europe). Per-page parse costs (v2 API tiers): Fast = 1 credit/page (~$0.00125), Cost-Effective = 3 credits/page (~$0.00375), Agentic = 10 credits/page (~$0.0125), Agentic Plus = 45 credits/page (~$0.056). Add-ons: layout extraction +3 credits/page; audio 3 credits/min; spreadsheets 1 credit/sheet. Subscription tiers: Free $0 (10K credits/mo), Starter $50/mo (40K credits, PAYG up to $500/mo), Pro $500/mo (400K credits, PAYG up to $5,000/mo), Enterprise custom.
backends.free_tier: 10,000 free credits per month on the Free plan (no card required); roughly 3,300 pages/mo at Cost-Effective (3 credits) or 10,000 pages at Fast (1 credit). Renews monthly.
backends.python_install: pip install llama-cloud (current/recommended SDK, v2-only, MIT, actively maintained; latest 2.9.0 as of 2026-06). NOTE: the older `pip install llama-cloud-services` (supports v1 + v2) is now DEPRECATED — maintained only until 2026-05-01, after which its repo is archived; migrate to llama-cloud.
backends.languages_note: Marketed as "100+ languages." No authoritative fixed language list is published; multilingual handling is delegated through an LLM/VLM orchestration layer rather than dedicated per-language OCR models. Documented examples include Latin, CJK (Japanese), Arabic, and French; in practice covers Latin, CJK, Arabic, Cyrillic, and Indic scripts via the underlying foundation models.
backends.accuracy_note: No single official CER/WER published by the vendor. Third-party RD-TableBench (Reducto, complex tables): LlamaParse Pro ~74.6% table similarity vs Reducto ~90.2% — competitive but behind best-in-class on hard tables. On OmniDocBench, LlamaIndex itself argues exact-match scoring penalizes its semantically-correct markdown (e.g. cited examples scoring 0.6344 / 0.3825 TEDS due to HTML-vs-LaTeX and cell-merge annotation mismatches), arguing the benchmark is saturated/misaligned rather than a true accuracy ceiling. Net: strong, layout-aware GenAI parsing; accuracy varies by tier (Fast text-only up to Agentic Plus) and document complexity; no standardized head-to-head CER/WER benchmark found that the vendor endorses.
backends.speed_note: Latency varies by tier: Fast is lowest-latency (plain-text, high-volume, text + spatial text only, no markdown); Agentic/Agentic Plus use VLMs/LLMs per page and are slower. Async job-based REST API; supports batching and auto mode routing.
backends.maturity_note: Active and widely adopted as of 2026-06: vendor cites 300k+ LlamaParse users and 1B+ documents processed. v2 Parse API + new SDKs (llama-cloud) shipped late 2025; llama-cloud-services on PyPI is regularly updated. Backed by LlamaIndex (well-funded OSS RAG framework, 25M+ monthly downloads).
backends.privacy_note: Cloud-hosted SaaS — documents are uploaded to LlamaCloud and processed remotely; data leaves the machine. EU data region available. Enterprise plan offers self-hosted / on-prem / VPC deployment options and stricter data-handling terms; default SaaS is multi-tenant.
pros: GenAI-native: produces clean, semantically structured markdown/JSON/HTML from very complex layouts (tables, charts, checkboxes, handwriting, multi-column) that classical OCR struggles with
Flexible cost/accuracy dial via tiers (Fast 1cr -> Agentic Plus 45cr/page) plus Auto Mode routing that can cut cost up to ~80%
Generous free tier (10K credits/month) and simple credit pricing make it easy to start and prototype
Custom parsing prompts and user-defined output schemas for tailored/structured extraction, plus 130+ input file types
Tight integration with the LlamaIndex RAG ecosystem and well-maintained Python/TS SDKs + REST API; returns bounding boxes (spatial text)
cons: Cloud-only SaaS by default — data leaves your machine; on-prem only on Enterprise, a non-starter for some privacy/regulated workloads
High-accuracy tiers (Agentic Plus 45 credits/page ~= $0.056/page) get expensive at scale, and per-document cost is hard to predict with Auto Mode
No exact-match accuracy leadership: third-party RD-TableBench shows it trailing Reducto on complex tables (~74.6% vs ~90.2%)
No documented fixed list of supported languages or per-field confidence scores; multilingual relies on opaque LLM/VLM routing
LLM/VLM-based parsing can hallucinate or reformat content (e.g. HTML vs LaTeX for formulas), and higher tiers add latency
v1 vs v2 API split and two overlapping SDKs (llama-cloud-services vs llama-cloud) add migration/integration friction
backends.best_for: Teams building RAG/agent pipelines on complex, visually rich documents (financial reports, scientific papers, invoices, insurance/healthcare forms) who want LLM-ready markdown/JSON without managing OCR infrastructure, and who can accept a cloud SaaS and tune the cost/accuracy tier per document.

backends.name: Mathpix (Snip + Convert API)
backends.price_note: As of 2026-06. One-time $19.99 API setup fee. Snip app: Free (10 PDF pages + 10 images/month, 2x with .edu email); Pro $4.99/mo or $49.90/yr (1,000 PDF pages + 5,000 images/month); Organization $9.99/mo for 2 users ($4.49/mo per extra user, $3.99 at 50+). On-prem/SCS self-hosted container is custom enterprise pricing.
backends.free_tier: Convert API: $29 free testing credit for new accounts (no time-limited trial otherwise). Snip app: permanent free plan with 10 PDF pages/month + 10 images/month (doubled with a .edu email).
backends.python_install: pip install mpxpy
backends.languages_note: Docs list 39 languages across 5 script families: Latin (English, French, Spanish, Portuguese, Italian, German, Vietnamese, Czech, Turkish, Hungarian, Danish, Dutch, Romanian, Polish, Croatian), Asian/Indic + CJK (Hindi/Devanagari, Korean/Hangul, Chinese simplified+traditional, Japanese Kanji/Hiragana/Katakana, Thai, Tamil, Telugu, Gujarati, Bengali), Cyrillic (Russian, Bulgarian, Serbian, Ukrainian, Belarusian), and Semitic (Arabic, Hebrew). Primary strength remains English + math; CJK and Cyrillic well supported. Note older marketing says "28 languages" and the site elsewhere claims "100+" — the docs page (39) is the authoritative count.
backends.accuracy_note: Strongest on math/formula recognition. On OmniDocBench (CVPR 2025), Mathpix is a top-tier specialized pipeline: formula recognition CDM ~86-87% (comparable to GPT-4o and UniMERNet), and it posts the best/near-best edit distance for Chinese text (~0.384 normalized edit distance reported). Overall full-page OCR edit-distance is competitive but now matched or exceeded by newer VLMs (GPT-4o) and PP-OCRv5 on general text NED. No single official vendor-published CER/WER number; figures here are from third-party OmniDocBench evaluations.
backends.speed_note: Image endpoint (v3/text, v3/latex) is synchronous and fast (sub-second to a few seconds per image). PDF endpoint (v3/pdf) is asynchronous — submit then poll for completion; multi-page documents take seconds to minutes depending on length. Batch endpoint available for high throughput.
backends.privacy_note: Cloud SaaS: images/PDFs are sent to Mathpix servers for processing. Mathpix states it does not use customer content to train models by default and offers data-retention controls; an on-premise self-hosted container (Mathpix SCS / OCR server) is available under enterprise contracts for fully on-prem processing where data never leaves the customer's infrastructure.
backends.maturity_note: Mature, actively maintained commercial product (founded ~2016). Snip desktop/mobile apps and Convert API in continuous development; "SuperNet" model line and Mathpix 4 are recent generations. Official Python SDK mpxpy on GitHub (Mathpix/mpxpy) and PyPI, actively updated. As of 2026-06.
pros: Best-in-class STEM/math OCR: converts printed and handwritten equations, chemistry (to SMILES/ChemDraw), and complex tables to LaTeX/MathML/Markdown with high fidelity
Rich output formats out of the box: LaTeX, Mathpix Markdown, DOCX, HTML, PDF, CSV/TSV tables, plus DOCX/PPTX/EPUB document conversion
Structured API: returns bounding boxes, per-token confidence scores, line data, and reading-order/layout structure for downstream processing
Low pay-as-you-go pricing (~$0.002/image, $0.005/PDF page) with $29 free credit and a permanent free Snip tier for evaluation
Official Python SDK (mpxpy) plus REST API, desktop/mobile Snip apps, and an on-prem container option for sensitive data
cons: Proprietary and closed-source; no model weights, and full local/offline use requires an enterprise on-prem contract
Cloud-by-default means documents leave your machine unless you pay for the self-hosted SCS container
General full-page text OCR is now matched or beaten by newer VLMs (GPT-4o) and open models (PP-OCRv5) on standard benchmarks — Mathpix's edge is specifically STEM/math, not generic OCR

backends.best_for: Digitizing STEM content — math/physics equations, chemistry structures, scientific tables, and handwritten notes — into LaTeX, Markdown, or DOCX, whether interactively via the Snip app or programmatically via the Convert API for document-processing pipelines.

backends.best_for: Teams that want fast, training-free structured-JSON extraction from business documents (invoices, receipts, IDs, bank statements, payslips, contracts) via a hosted API, with prebuilt endpoints plus custom/generated models and a generous 250-page/month free tier — and who are comfortable sending documents to a cloud service.
pros: Prebuilt endpoints for many common business docs (invoice, receipt, passport/ID, bank statement, payslip, etc.) return clean structured JSON with no model training required
docTI / V2 is training-free (LLM + CV) and handles arbitrary layouts, file formats, and many languages/scripts out of the box
